facts: The three main aims of a cardiovascular history: establish the indications for surgery; identify issues that need management outside standard protocols; define the preoperative estimate of risk (mortality, stroke, etc.).
Angina is frequently not the classic 'central, crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw and down the left arm'.
Angina may present as heaviness, indigestion, isolated arm, neck or jaw discomfort, nausea, or fatigue.
Ask about precipitants of angina: exertion, stress, emotion and cold air.
Ask about relieving factors of angina (rest, sublingual nitroglycerine (NTG)) and how many times a day NTG spray is used.
Angina is graded (Box 1.1); class III and IV (heart failure) symptoms are associated with increased risk.
Ask about exertional dyspnea and classify it (Box 1.1); heart failure is defined as class III or IV symptoms.
Other precipitants of breathlessness to ask about: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, palpitations, chest infections, COPD, pulmonary embolism, medication such as beta-blockers.
Associated symptoms of breathlessness to ask about: peripheral edema, palpitations, wheeze and sputum.
Relieving factors of breathlessness to ask about: NTG, rest, sitting up.
Previous MI: document the number, dates and anatomy of previous MIs; check the chart and EKG (Q waves).
Risk of surgery is higher after a recent ST segment elevation MI (STEMI) than after a non-ST segment elevation MI (NSTEMI).
Risk of surgery is highest early after MI, falling after 1 week.
Previous chest surgery: ask, check the chart, and look carefully at the whole chest and back for scars.
Previous cardiac surgery is associated with incremental operative mortality and requires several changes to the standard operative approach.

Most patients with previous cardiac surgery should undergo CT chest (requires iv contrast) to evaluate the relationship of the aorta and right ventricle to the sternum, and the location of patent bypass grafts.
Obtain the operative report of the previous surgery.
Box 1.1: the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) classification applies to angina only.
CCS class I: no angina with ordinary activity.
CCS class II: slight limitation of ordinary activity.
CCS class III: marked limitation of ordinary activity.
CCS class IV: angina on minimal exertion or at rest.
Box 1.1: the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification applies to dyspnea and/or angina.
NYHA class I: no limitation during ordinary activity (asymptomatic).
NYHA class II: slight limitation during ordinary activity.
NYHA class III: marked limitation of ordinary activity.
NYHA class IV: no physical activity without symptoms.
Previous percutaneous interventions: note LV function and coronary anatomy from the angiography report.
Document the number, dates, type and result of previous percutaneous interventions (angioplasty or stenting).
Emergency surgery after failed percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is high risk.
Recent PCI usually mandates at least 1 month of clopidogrel, and can impact the conduct of coronary bypass surgery.
'Black-outs' may be a result of epilepsy, TIAs, hypoglycemia, or vasovagal syndromes (standing, emotion, coughing, micturition).
True cardiac syncope from aortic stenosis is usually exertional.
Syncope when the patient is sitting or lying suggests arrhythmias.
Dizziness may be associated with syncope (presyncopal episodes) but is fairly non-specific.
Common causes of dizziness are antianginals, antihypertensives and diuretics causing postural hypotension.
Dizziness may reflect low cardiac output states (failure, arrhythmias, ischemia) or cerebrovascular disease.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy is probably an under-recognized cause of dizziness.
To the patient, palpitations may be skipped beats, tachycardia, irregular rhythm, or awareness of their heart, particularly at night.
Rapid onset and offset of palpitations suggests paroxysmal arrhythmias; gradual onset and offset suggests sinus tachycardia.
Preoperative atrial fibrillation may require ablation and/or left atrial appendage ligation, and warfarin.
Peripheral edema may be associated with changes in diuretic therapy, weight gain and exacerbations of dyspnea, and helps quantify the heart failure.
Extracardiac arteriopathy: ask specifically about TIAs, strokes, claudication and vascular interventions.
A history of TIAs warrants a carotid duplex to exclude carotid disease, which may be an indication for carotid intervention.
Extracardiac arteriopathy is important for risk scoring.
Extracardiac arteriopathy affects the risk of stroke and limb ischemia quoted when consenting the patient.
Extracardiac arteriopathy influences the choice of conduit and the cannulation site.
Reversible coronary risk factors that should be addressed in hospital: smoking, hypercholesterolemia, obesity, hypertension and diabetes.
Irreversible coronary risk factors: male sex, age and family history.
Be precise about smoking: 'non-smoker' is not the same as 'smoked 60 a day, gave up 2 weeks ago'.
Valve patients: note the type and degree of valve disease, and LV function, from the echo.
Ask valve patients about rheumatic disease and endocarditis.
Check that valve patients have been recently cleared by a dentist; edentulous patients do not need to be seen by a dentist.
Check that valve patients have no active sources of infection.
Valve patients should have had an angiogram if they are males over 45 years, postmenopausal females, or have angina-type symptoms or multiple coronary risk factors.
Check that the type of valve replacement has been discussed with the valve patient.

Main aims of the systems enquiry: identify problems that alter standard perioperative management; identify contraindications to elective surgery; identify problems that could potentially delay discharge.

Previous medical history: ask about other medical problems, then repeat the question by asking about any hospital admissions other than for the heart and any operations ever; be persistent, as patients often forget important chronic illnesses and operations.
Previous chest radiotherapy mandates a CT scan: the aorta may be calcified.
Malignant disease should be carefully evaluated: in most cases metastatic spread is a relative contraindication to cardiac surgery.
Thyroid disease may dictate the choice of antiarrhythmic.
Patients with hip replacements should be transferred with a pillow between their legs: adducting the hip may result in dislocation.
Patients with blood dyscrasias (thrombocytopenia, factor deficiencies, thrombophilias) should be reviewed by a hematologist.
Take full details of all drugs, doses and regimens, and of allergies to drugs, iodine, contrast and fish.
Fish allergy matters because protamine is made from salmon sperm.
Latex allergies require changes to equipment: warn the operating room.
A history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia may require non-heparin (bivalirudin or argatroban) bypass, which mandates careful preplanning.
Continue antianginals until surgery, and stop them postoperatively.
Continue beta-blockers until surgery, and reintroduce them postoperatively as blood pressure and rhythm permit.
Stop ACE inhibitors 24-48 hours before surgery to avoid profound peripheral dilatation in the immediate postoperative period.
Aspirin and clopidogrel are discontinued by many surgeons 5-10 days preoperatively, as they predispose to increased postoperative bleeding.
Stopping aspirin and clopidogrel carries a slightly higher risk of acute ischemic events; in high-risk patients (e.g. recent PCI, tight left main stem) they may be continued.
Warfarin should be stopped 5 days before surgery.
In patients at higher risk of thromboembolic events (e.g. prior TIA, DVT), admission 24-48 hours pre-op may be required for iv heparin.
Steroids should be reduced where possible preoperatively.
Patients taking more than 5 mg prednisone daily should be prescribed hydrocortisone 50-100 mg iv 6-hourly (or an equivalent dose by continuous infusion) for 48 hours, starting with the premedication.
Perioperative steroid cover is given to avoid Addisonian crisis as a result of adrenal suppression.
Withhold long-acting hypoglycemics on the morning of surgery and commence an insulin sliding scale where appropriate.
Jehovah's witness patients do not accept blood or blood products, and some may not agree to the use of cell salvage.
Jehovah's witness patients must be identified preoperatively, counselled, and their preferences clearly documented.
In Jehovah's witness patients every effort should be made to ensure a preoperative hematocrit more than 40%; several weeks of erythropoietin therapy may be indicated.
Heavy or binge drinkers are at risk of alcohol withdrawal.
Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and prolongs the QT (so it is not the drug for alcohol withdrawal).
For alcohol withdrawal prescribe diazepam 2 mg orally 8-hourly, thiamine and folate.
If the patient lives alone, plan for rehabilitation.
If the patient mobilizes with a walking stick or frame, contact physiotherapists early, as sternal union may be compromised even if mobility is not.
An active upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) is sufficient reason to cancel the operation, so ask about cough, colds and sputum.
If you suspect a URTI, measure temperature, CRP and white cell count, and get a chest X-ray.
Assess COPD by asking about hospital admissions, inhalers, nebulizers and home oxygen.
If dyspnea is the prominent symptom and the patient has COPD, get lung function tests including blood gases.
Cardiac surgery patients are at risk of upper GI bleeds from peptic ulcer disease, prolonged ileus, and acute deterioration in pre-existing disease (e.g. pancreatitis, cholecystitis).
Ask specifically about GI problems, particularly dyspepsia, ulcers and pancreatitis.
Start all patients on prophylactic proton pump inhibitors (PPIs).
Make a note on the drug chart to avoid NSAID analgesics in at-risk patients.
In at-risk (GI) patients aspirin should be enteric coated and given with food.
Check the notes for renal dysfunction; if there has been an acute deterioration it may be worth delaying the patient to optimize it.
Optimizing renal function: stop nephrotoxic drugs including ACE inhibitors and NSAID analgesia, start iv fluids with careful fluid balance, and in some cases dialysis.
Dialysis patients should be dialysed the morning of surgery or the night before.
Patients undergoing preoperative cardiac catheterization are at particular risk of temporary renal impairment from hypovolemia (preprocedure fasting) combined with nephrotoxic contrast.
Prescribe iv fluid in patients with borderline renal function, and consider iv acetylcysteine prior to contrast studies.
Patients with a history suggestive of prostatic enlargement should be warned that they may need a suprapubic catheter.
Neurological history: identify TIAs, strokes and residual deficit.
Identify dementia: in advanced cases it is a contraindication to cardiac surgery.
Main purposes of the examination: identify disease that needs further investigation and management; help plan surgery; identify problems that may delay recovery.
For the average elective patient a shortened version of the full cardiovascular examination is sufficient (Box 1.2).
Box 1.2 short examination: assess pulse rate and rhythm.
Box 1.2: assess the jugular venous pressure with the patient at 45 degrees.
Box 1.2: auscultate heart sounds, carotids and breath sounds; look for scars.
Box 1.2: examine the abdomen (tenderness, hernias, organomegaly, scars).
Box 1.2: feel peripheral pulses including the abdominal aorta.
General inspection from the end of the bed: comfortable at rest, requiring oxygen, well or moribund, obese or cachexic.
Features of Down's syndrome suggest atrial or ventricular septal defect (ASD/VSD).
Features of Marfan syndrome suggest aortic aneurysms, dissection and incompetence.
Position the patient at 45 degrees in the bed.
Hands and forearms: look for nicotine staining and tendon xanthoma.
Stigmata of endocarditis in the hands: splinter hemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions.
Osler's nodes are tender lumps in the fingertip pulps.
Janeway lesions are red macules on the palms or flexor aspects of the wrist.
Petechiae may be present in infective endocarditis.
Note rate and rhythm at the radial pulse, and character and volume at the brachial or carotid pulse.
Aortic stenosis classically has a slow rising, thready pulse.
Aortic incompetence has a large volume bounding pulse.
Feel the peripheral pulses including the abdominal aorta.
Uncontrolled hypertension: systolic more than 180 mmHg should be treated with nifedipine 10 mg sublingually preoperatively.
A wide pulse pressure is suggestive of aortic incompetence.
Use a broad cuff for fat arms, as BP will otherwise be underestimated.
Check BP in both arms if aortic dissection or coarctation is suspected.
Malar flush (cyanosis in a butterfly rash distribution) is characteristic of mitral stenosis.
Jaundice may be caused by hemolysis from prosthetic heart valves.
Xanthelasma and corneal arcus are common signs of hyperlipidemia.
Roth spots may be seen in infective endocarditis.
Rarely, Argyll Robertson pupils are a feature of syphilitic aortic incompetence.
Mouth: check for central cyanosis by examining the tongue and gums.
Look for the high arched palate of Marfan.
Check for poor dentition, particularly in valve patients.
Neck: assess the jugular venous pulse with the patient at 45 degrees.
Inspect the chest for scars (left and right lateral thoracotomy, median sternotomy), ICD and pacemaker insertion, pectus and visible pulsations.
Expose the patient adequately or you will miss these chest signs.
The apex beat is the point furthest from the manubrium where the heart can be felt.
The apex beat is normally in the 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line.
The apex beat is shifted laterally in cardiomegaly or mediastinal shift.
Aortic stenosis and hypertensive cardiomyopathy result in a sustained, forceful apex beat.
A dilated LV (e.g. aortic regurgitation) normally has a downwards displaced apex beat.
In mitral stenosis the apex beat is described as tapping.
A left parasternal heave may be felt in right ventricular hypertrophy.
Time heart sounds against the radial pulse.
Use the bell for low-pitched sounds and the diaphragm for high-pitched sounds.
Listen over the apex (diaphragm and bell), upper and lower left sternal borders, under the clavicles, over the carotids, and in the axilla (diaphragm with or without bell).
Then listen again at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position.
Then listen at the lower left sternal border with the patient sitting forward in full expiration.
Murmurs can be graded on a scale of 1-6.
Grade 1 murmur: just audible in a quiet room with the patient breath holding.
Grade 3 murmur: easy to hear, without a thrill.
Grade 6 murmur: audible without a stethoscope.
Murmurs and carotid bruits need ultrasound imaging.
Ejection systolic murmurs: aortic stenosis, aortic sclerosis, pulmonary stenosis, ASD, 'innocent' flow murmur.
The aortic stenosis murmur is loudest in the aortic area in expiration and radiates to the carotids.
Causes of an 'innocent' flow murmur: anemia, hyperthyroidism, pregnancy.
Pansystolic murmurs: mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation, VSD, patent ductus arteriosus.
The mitral regurgitation murmur is loudest at the apex and radiates to the axilla.
Early diastolic murmurs: aortic regurgitation, pulmonary regurgitation.
Mid diastolic murmurs: mitral stenosis, tricuspid stenosis, Austin Flint murmur of aortic regurgitation.
Conduit: stand the patient up so that you can see both legs from ankle to groin.
Look for varicosities and decide which distribution they are in (long or short saphenous).
Allen's test tests the suitability of the radial artery.

Allen's test: the patient clenches the fist tightly, both radial and ulnar pulses are occluded, the patient opens the hand, and you note how long the palm takes to pink up once the ulnar occlusion is released.
A refill time less than 5 seconds is suitable for radial artery harvest.
General examination: listen to the chest and palpate the abdomen.
Routine preoperative investigations include a complete blood count (CBC).
Coagulation screen: activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) and prothrombin time (PT); INR if taking warfarin.
Biochemistry (Chem 7): Na, K, Cl, HCO3, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, glucose.
Liver function tests (LFTs) are a routine preoperative investigation.
Cross-match 4 units plus fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and platelets in reoperations or thoracoabdominals.
MRSA screening swab, urinalysis, pregnancy test and sickle cell testing are routine.
Raised Na (more than 145 mmol/L): commonly diarrhea, vomiting; less commonly diabetes insipidus.
Raised Na management: oral water or iv 5% dextrose; discuss with the anesthesiologist.
Low Na (less than 130 mmol/L): commonly diuretics, diarrhea, vomiting.
Low Na, less commonly: congestive cardiac failure, cirrhosis, renal failure (printed as 'nephritic syndromes'), Addison's, SIADH.
Low Na management: assess renal function and treat accordingly; fluid restrict if appropriate; discuss with the anesthesiologist.
Raised K (more than 5 mmol/L): commonly K-sparing diuretics and ACE inhibitors, excess K therapy, artifact (hemolysis in the tube).
Raised K, less commonly: renal failure, diabetic acidosis, Addison's disease.
It should be possible to correct hyperkalemia over 12 h.
Low K (less than 3.5 mmol/L): commonly diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea.
Low K, less commonly: Conn's, Cushing's syndromes, renal tubular failure.
It should be possible to correct hypokalemia over 12 h.
Raised creatinine (more than 1.2 mg/dL) and BUN (more than 21 mg/dL): renal impairment.
A disproportionately raised urea suggests dehydration as the primary cause.
An isolated raised urea ('U') occurs with thiazide diuretics, gout, lymphoma, leukemia.
Raised LFTs, bilirubin or gamma GT: common drug causes are paracetamol, OCP, co-amoxiclav, chlorpromazine, erythromycin.
Other common causes of raised LFTs: hemolysis, viral hepatitis, gallstones, Gilbert's syndrome, sepsis, alcohol.
Less commonly, raised LFTs are due to malignancy causing biliary tract obstruction.
Raised LFTs: ask about iv drug use, transfusions, travel, alcohol.
Raised LFTs: examine the abdomen for enlarged spleen or liver and signs of chronic liver disease; test urine for bilirubin and urobilinogen.
Raised LFTs: request a liver ultrasound; consider serology.
The decision to cancel surgery to investigate or treat a screening abnormality weighs the risk of delaying surgery against the increased risk of surgery.
A symptomatic, unstable patient with a tight LMS lesion is less likely to be cancelled for a mild neutrophilia than an elective valve patient.
Discuss any move to cancel with the surgical team.
Low Hb (less than 9.5 g/dL) with MCV less than 75: iron deficiency, thalassemia.
Low Hb with MCV 75-95: chronic disease, renal failure, bone marrow failure, hemolysis, hypothyroidism, dilutional (acute).
Low Hb with MCV more than 95: low B12 or folate, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasias, bone marrow infiltration.
Undiagnosed iron deficiency should be fully investigated, as GI malignancy is a common cause in this age group.
Treat the causes of anemia where possible and avoid transfusion unless Hb is very low.
The perfusionist may want extra blood to prime the pump.
Raised Hb (more than 14 g/dL), relative (reduced plasma volume): dehydration (alcohol and diuretics).
Raised Hb, absolute (raised red cell mass): primary polycythemia rubra vera; secondary to smoking, COPD, altitude, tumours.
Polycythemia vera (PCV) patients may need formal anticoagulation postoperatively to prevent thromboembolic events.
Raised WCC (more than 12x10^9/L), neutrophilia: bacterial sepsis, trauma, surgery, burns, inflammation, MI, polymyalgia, steroids, hemorrhage.
Lymphocytosis (printed 'lymphophilia'): viral infection (EBV, CMV), chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
Eosinophilia: asthma, allergy, parasitic infections, eczema, malignancy.
Raised WCC: recheck history and examination for evidence of sepsis, take temperature, look at the CXR and urine dipsticks.
Elective valve patients with a raised WCC: check with the team; surgery may be cancelled.
If the raised WCC is due to a URTI, start antibiotics and recheck the WCC in 2-3 weeks.
Low WCC (less than 2x10^9/L): rarely neutropenic sepsis, steroids, sulfonamides, SLE.
Low WCC: discuss with a hematologist; it is an emergency in sepsis.
Raised platelets (more than 400x10^9/L): essential thrombocythemia, sepsis, inflammatory disease (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis).
Of patients with raised platelets, 50% have malignancy.
Raised platelets: discuss with a hematologist.
Low platelets (less than 120x10^9/L): heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, sepsis and DIC, drugs, SLE, lymphoma, bone marrow failure.
Low platelets: discontinue heparin and request a heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) screen.
Low platelets in septic patients: send fibrin degradation products; request platelets.
Raised PT: warfarin, low vitamin K, liver disease.
Raised APTT: heparin, low factor VIII or IX.
Abnormal clotting: investigate as for liver disease, measure clotting factors, talk to a hematologist.
Atypical antibodies may mean more time and further samples are required to obtain blood that gives a satisfactory cross-match.

facts: The standard chest film is the posteroanterior (PA) view.
PA film: the patient stands facing the film, clasping it in both arms; X-rays pass from posterior to anterior.
Films are taken in full inspiration to maximize the size of the lung fields.
The anteroposterior (AP) view is used for portable films in immobile patients: plate under the back, X-rays pass anterior to posterior.
PA advantage: the scapulae are rotated away, so they obscure the lung fields less.
PA advantage: the heart shadow is smaller, so more of the lung fields are visible.
PA advantage: the relative sizes of lung fields and cardiac silhouette can be reliably used to comment on cardiomegaly and mediastinal widening.
Lateral films further define abnormalities identified in the lung fields on PA and AP films.
A left lateral film defines abnormalities in the left thorax: left side against the film, labelled 'L'; right laterals are taken similarly.
CXR system: confirm the patient's name and age and the date of the film.
Define the film: AP, PA or lateral; erect or supine; contrast or plain.
Check that the film is oriented correctly.
Alignment: clavicles and ribs symmetrically aligned with the sternum and spinous processes.
The film should show all of the lung fields from apex to costophrenic angle.
Adequate exposure: you should see the vertebral bodies through the heart.
Comment on presence and position of ET and NG tubes, catheters (PA or central line), clips, drains, prosthetic valves, rings, wires.
Bones: look for fractures and dislocations, lytic lesions, calcification, erosions and extra ribs.
The ribs are easier to see posteriorly than anteriorly.
Assess the soft tissue shadows of the neck, chest wall and breasts.
The right hemidiaphragm is normally one rib higher than the left.
Mediastinal shadow: aortic knob, pulmonary trunk, LA appendage, LV, IVC, right atrium, SVC.
Then assess the airways (trachea, main bronchi), lung fields, fissures and vascularity of the lung fields.
A normal deep breath inflates the lungs to the 10th rib posteriorly or the 6th rib anteriorly.
The trachea should be midline; opacities should be symmetrical.
It takes 400 mL of fluid to blunt the costophrenic angles.
In the supine patient a fluid level is replaced by diffuse opacity.
If one hemithorax is more opaque: a collection on the opaque side, or a pneumothorax on the other side.
Fig 1.1a normal PA film, left mediastinal border from above down: aortic knuckle, pulmonary trunk, left atrial appendage, left ventricle.
Fig 1.1a right mediastinal border: superior vena cava, right atrium, with the inferior vena cava below.
Fig 1.1a also labels the trachea, carina, right costophrenic angle and apex of the right lung.
Fig 1.1a bony landmarks: a spinous process (legend: T12), 1st left rib, left clavicle, body of left scapula, left 8th rib.
Fig 1.1a labels the right and left hemidiaphragms.
Fig 1.1b lateral film labels the manubriosternal junction, thoracic vertebral bodies, body of scapula, right and left hemidiaphragms.
Fig 1.1b lateral film heart: right ventricle anteriorly, left ventricle, left atrium posteriorly.
Fig 1.1b lateral film also labels the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, proximal and distal trachea, distal aortic arch, aortopulmonary window.
A portable chest X-ray is done on immediate arrival in the ICU.
Fig 1.2a early postoperative film shows NG tube, ET tube, PA catheter and sheath, sternal wires, EKG leads, chest tubes and a bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement.
The ET tube should be 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the carina.
The NG tube should be visible in the stomach.
The PA catheter is usually in the right pulmonary artery; check it is not coiled, in too far, or malpositioned (e.g. in the IVC).
Look for collections (may be just diffuse haze in supine patients), pneumothorax and lobar collapse.
Pericardial effusion on CXR: a globular heart shadow.
CT and echo are diagnostic of pericardial effusion.
Echo is required for the diagnosis of tamponade.
Pleural effusion in an erect patient: a concave upwards meniscus suggests fluid.
A flat fluid level suggests hydropneumothorax.
Fig 1.3a-d normal contrast CT labels the trachea, right and left lungs, body of T3 and esophagus.
Upper mediastinal CT: SVC full of contrast, brachiocephalic artery, left common carotid and left subclavian artery.
Fig 1.3b-c: the aortic arch; lower, the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, descending aorta and carina.
Fig 1.3d cardiac level: left atrium (posterior), right atrium, right ventricle (anterior) and the hemiazygous vein.
Fig 1.3e: CT with iv contrast showing a type A dissection.
Fig 1.3f: the arrow shows an obvious dissection flap; the flap is often less prominent and more concave.
CT uses the same radiation as standard X-rays but moves the X-ray source round the patient.
CT attenuation of each point is measured in Hounsfield units (HU): water is 0 HU; the scale runs from +1000 (white) to -1000 (black).
Bone is +400 to +1000 HU (white); contrast is +800 HU (white).
Soft tissue is +40 to +80 HU (gray); lung is -500 HU (gray to black).
The eye cannot distinguish 2000 shades of gray, so a limited range of HU (window width, WW) is displayed around a central window level (WL), chosen by the tissue of interest.
A mediastinal or soft tissue window has a window level of +40 HU.
A lung window has a window level of -600 HU and shows detailed lung parenchyma that cannot be seen on soft tissue windows.
IV contrast is used to define vascular structures on CT.
Conventional CT: the X-ray source and detectors cannot rotate continuously; the table moves the patient a set distance, stopping between slices.

Spiral CT (which has replaced most conventional scanners) uses slip rings that remove the physical connection between X-ray tube and power cables, so the ring rotates in one direction indefinitely while the table moves continuously.
Spiral CT advantage: faster, higher-resolution images allowing angiography, e.g. coronary and pulmonary angiography and standard vascular views.
Spiral CT advantage: images in any plane and 3D images can be constructed.
Multislice CT has several rows of detectors instead of the single row of conventional and spiral scanners, and much faster tube rotation.
Multislice CT acquires images several times faster than spiral CT, so it is used in unstable and uncooperative patients and for vascular imaging, minimizing scan time and movement artefact.
Multislice CT resolution is significantly better, allowing video footage, e.g. of valves.
Chest CT in reoperations identifies vascular structures at particular risk during sternal re-entry, e.g. patent grafts, aorta, RV.
Valve patients at low risk of coronary disease may have CT coronary angiography rather than cardiac catheterization to evaluate coronary disease preoperatively.
CT angiography is very specific and sensitive for coronary disease.
Any significant abnormality on CT coronary angiography should be evaluated with standard coronary angiography, so there is little to gain from CT in higher-risk patients.
Contrast load and radiation exposure are very similar for invasive and CT angiography.
Chest CT is used for diagnosis and evaluation of aortic aneurysm and dissection.
Chest CT is used to evaluate mediastinitis, sternal dehiscence and PE.

Fig. 1.4a: non-contrast chest CT (mediastinal and lung windows) of a large ascending and descending aortic aneurysm shows calcification in the aortic wall but little other information about the vessel lumen.
Fig. 1.4b: in the same patient, IV contrast clearly shows a type B dissection with intraluminal thrombus in the descending aorta.
Fig. 1.4c: 3D reconstruction of an aneurysmal ascending aorta shows the right coronary artery in the atrioventricular groove.
Cardiac catheterization may be right and/or left heart, diagnostic or therapeutic.
Left heart catheterization is via the femoral or radial artery.
Left heart catheterization measures LA, LV and aortic pressures and transmitral and transaortic pressure gradients.
Left heart catheterization allows calculation of mitral and aortic valve areas.
Left heart catheterization allows coronary angiography (the commonest indication) and ventriculography, which requires substantially more contrast.
Therapeutic left heart procedures: PCI, percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty (BMV), TAVI, LA appendage occlusion.
Right heart catheterization is via the femoral, internal jugular or subclavian vein and is essentially the same as floating a Swan-Ganz catheter.
Right heart catheterization measures RA, RV and PA pressures, pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) and saturations including SvO2 (mixed venous oxygen saturation).
Right heart catheterization allows calculation of PVR (pulmonary vascular resistance; printed 'peripheral'), cardiac output and shunts.
Right heart catheterization allows pulmonary angiography.
Right heart catheterization allows transseptal puncture for LA access.
Contraindications to catheterization are few; the patient may be too unwell to tolerate it, e.g. acute type A dissection.

Patients with AS or mobile vegetations should not have ventriculography or pull-back gradients: crossing the aortic valve carries a risk of stroke, and hemodynamic data can be obtained more safely by echocardiography.
Patients with renal dysfunction should not have ventriculograms, as the increased contrast load will exacerbate renal impairment significantly.
Coronary angiography technique: patient usually awake but sedated and supine; access via a sheath using a modified Seldinger technique.
Radio-opaque contrast is injected into the coronary ostia in turn via a size 4 Judkins catheter (2-3 mm diameter).
The X-ray tube and camera are opposite each other on a C-arm, rotated cranially and caudally and from left to right to give a range of views of the coronary anatomy.
Biplane imaging uses two cameras to obtain simultaneous images from two different angles, reducing radiation exposure.
Moving images are captured on digital CDs, which have superseded cine film.
Patients may be given 300 mg of clopidogrel or 75 mg of aspirin pre- and post-PCI.
Complications requiring emergency bypass surgery (LAD dissection, acute LAD occlusion, cardiac tamponade) occur in 1 in 1000 catheterizations.
Major adverse events (e.g. stroke) occur in 1%; death in 0.01%.
Failure to occlude the puncture site after removal can cause extensive hematoma, which may be retroperitoneal if the femoral puncture is high.
Look at each lesion in several views and at the whole film.
Eccentric plaques look most significant viewed end on and may almost disappear when viewed perpendicularly.
Lesions are compared with adjacent 'normal' segments: in diffusely diseased vessels this can lead to underestimating severity.
A 50% reduction in vessel diameter corresponds to a 75% reduction in cross-sectional area.
A 70% reduction in vessel diameter corresponds to a 90% reduction in cross-sectional area.
Fig. 1.5b: a 90% diameter narrowing corresponds to a 99% area narrowing.
A stenosis is significant if it is more than 50% of the lumen diameter, as it reduces the normal 3-4 times flow reserve.
A stenosis of more than 70% lumen diameter eliminates any capacity to increase flow above resting flow.
A stenosis of more than 90% usually means TIMI grade 1 or 2 flow.
Occluded vessels frequently fill late, retrogradely, from shots of other vessels: most commonly the PDA and RCA from the LAD, and sometimes the LAD from the PDA.
Beware mistaking a large diagonal for a completely occluded LAD: always look at the LAO view before commenting on the LAD.
Start with a summary after viewing all views, e.g. 'a 75-year-old male with 3-vessel disease and moderate LV...'.
Describe the LMS, best seen in the RAO view and the LAO caudal.
Describe the circumflex system, best seen in the RAO view.
Describe the LAD and diagonals, best seen in the LAO cranial.
Describe the RCA and PDA, and the dominance.
Describe the ventricular function, any regional akinesia, MR, and calcification of the coronary vessels or valves.
Fig. 1.5a: the X-ray box and camera are oriented for the various views: PA, RAO and LAO, with cranial angulation.
Recognizing angiographic views and vessels rapidly becomes pattern recognition, but a systematic approach helps avoid common mistakes.
Identify each view, look at all the views, look at each vessel in multiple views, and look at the whole clip for each view (some vessels only fill late).
In a RAO view the ribs go down to the right of the image, which is on the right of the spine (catheter in aorta).
In a LAO view the ribs go down to the left of the image, which is on the left of the spine (catheter in aorta).
In cranial views the diaphragm is superimposed over most of the picture; in caudal views it is hardly seen.
The circumflex is the vessel closest to the spine (or the catheter in the descending aorta) in every image.
The LAD travels towards the apex, is usually the longest vessel, and has septals coming off it at 90 degrees.

Fig. 1.6a: RAO view of the left coronary tree showing LMS disease; the circumflex is always the most posterior vessel, closest to the spine and the descending aorta, where the catheter can usually be seen.
Fig. 1.6b: RAO view of the right coronary tree showing proximal RCA stenosis; short septals coming off the PDA at 90 degrees distinguish the PDA from the LVB.
Branches of the RCA in order: 1) conus branch, 2) SA nodal branch, 3) RV branch, 4) acute marginal.
5) The AV nodal artery arises from the RCA in 60%.
6) In right-dominant patients (85%) the RCA bifurcates into the PDA, which gives off inferior septals at 90 degrees, and 7) the LVB or posterolateral branches.
Proximal RCA is up to the RV branch, mid RCA up to the acute marginal, and distal RCA up to the bifurcation.
The LMS bifurcates (occasionally trifurcates, with a ramus intermediate branch) into the LAD and circumflex.
The LAD gives off septals at 90 degrees and diagonals.
The circumflex gives off obtuse marginals (OMs) and may give rise to the AV nodal artery (40%).
In left-dominant patients (10%) the circumflex gives the PDA and the LVB or posterolateral branches.
Proximal LAD is up to the 1st septal, mid LAD until the 2nd diagonal, and distal LAD after the 2nd diagonal.
Fig. 1.7: the five common angiographic views: RAO and LAO views of the right coronary artery; RAO, LAO and LAO caudal ('spider view') of the left coronary system.
Angiography may misrepresent the severity of coronary stenosis; additional information comes from pressure measurements, e.g. fractional flow reserve (FFR), and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS).
When echocardiography is equivocal, cardiac catheterization gives useful additional information on severity of valve lesions, pulmonary hypertension, ventricular function and intracardiac shunts.
FFR is essentially the ratio between the blood pressure proximal and distal to a lesion when flow is maximal.
An FFR below 75% (i.e. less than 75% of maximal flow in a non-diseased coronary) indicates a significant lesion.
Some data suggest it is safe to watch (rather than intervene) in patients with higher FFRs.
FFR is measured at maximal flow induced by adenosine or papaverine (4-5 times resting flow in the normal subject), hence it assesses coronary reserve.
TIMI 0 (no perfusion): absence of antegrade flow beyond a lesion.
TIMI 1 (penetration without perfusion): incomplete filling of the distal coronary bed.
TIMI 2 (partial reperfusion): delayed but complete filling distally.
Transaortic gradient: LV pressure is measured with either simultaneous aortic pressure distal to the valve (mean and peak-to-peak gradients) or 'pull-back' of the catheter into the aorta.
The most physiologic aortic valve gradient is the mean gradient.
Mitral gradients are measured by simultaneous recording of PAWP or LA pressure (obtained by transseptal puncture) and LV end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP).
Valve area is estimated with the Gorlin equation (essentially valve area = flow/velocity), or area = cardiac output / square root of pressure gradient.
Accurate cardiac output estimation is critical and particularly open to error in low cardiac output states, when dobutamine stress testing can be used as a diagnostic adjunct.
Grossman grade I regurgitation: faint opacification of the proximal chamber, clears with one beat.
Grossman grade II: opacification of the proximal chamber less than the distal chamber.
Grossman grade III: opacification of the proximal chamber equals the distal chamber.
Grossman grade IV: complete dense opacification of the proximal chamber, with a constant density greater than in the distal chamber.
There are multiple methods of calculating cardiac output during catheterization, all with potential errors.

Thermodilution: a bolus of normal saline is injected into the proximal port, a gradient between this and a distal port is measured and entered into an equation incorporating the specific gravity and temperatures of the fluid and the patient's blood.
Sources of error in thermodilution: TR, incorrect injection technique and low cardiac output.
Fick principle: the uptake (or release) of a substance (usually VO2) equals the arteriovenous concentration gradient times the cardiac output.
In most labs VO2 is not measured but assumed to be 125 mL/m2.
The Fick method is more accurate than thermodilution in low output states.
The Fick method should not be used in MR or AI, or in patients receiving supplemental oxygen.
Angiographic methods trace the LV end-diastolic and end-systolic images and convert them to volume using modelling.
PVR = (mPAP - mLAP)/CO; PAWP is substituted for LA pressure in the absence of pulmonary disease.
Fixed pulmonary hypertension cannot be reversed with NTG, inhaled NO, Flolan or exercise.
Cardiac catheterization is used to differentiate restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis.
Shunts are detected and quantified by blood oximetry sampling from IVC, SVC, multiple RA locations, PA, coronary sinus and artery.
Qp:Qs = (SaO2 - MVO2)/(PVO2 - PAO2) (brackets as evidently meant; printed without them).
Fig. 1.8 (quantifying valve stenosis at catheterization), example aortic gradients: peak instantaneous aortic gradient 100 mmHg, peak-to-peak aortic gradient 50 mmHg, mean aortic gradient 60 mmHg.
Fig. 1.8: the mean transmitral gradient is the area between the LA and LV pressure traces.
Echocardiography is ultrasound used to assess cardiac conditions.
There are two main approaches: transthoracic (TTE) and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE).
Box 1.2 terms for the modalities in common use: B-mode, M-mode, D-mode (Doppler), colour flow imaging and 3D echo.
B-mode (brightness mode), also called 2D or real-time, provides a 2D grayscale picture of a single plane across the heart.
In B-mode the intensity of the echo is related to the brightness of the signal.
M-mode (motion mode) is more accurate than B-mode, so it is used for measurements.
M-mode only yields a 1D image: structures plotted on the y-axis against time on the x-axis.
D-mode (Doppler) uses Doppler frequency shifts to measure flow velocities and hence calculate gradients and valve areas.
In Doppler only moving targets are displayed.
Duplex US combines Doppler and grayscale images to correlate flow with fixed structures.
Colour flow imaging is a colour-enhanced duplex Doppler echo combining M-mode and D-mode with blood flow imaging.
Most systems code blood flow away from the transducer as blue and towards the transducer as red (BART).
3D echo allows 3D visualization of cardiac structures and is particularly useful for viewing mitral valve morphology.
Echo ultrasound is a waveform of 2-5 MHz that passes through tissues and is reflected from tissue interfaces.
Piezoelectric crystals act as transducers, generating and detecting US by converting electrical to mechanical energy and vice versa; reflected waves are calibrated to form an image.
Doppler effect: waves reflected from a moving target increase in frequency if it moves towards the source and decrease if it moves away.
The Doppler shift is proportional to the speed of the object and can be quantified as an audible signal or colour.
The frequencies used cannot penetrate air or bone, which explains the need for certain views to assess some structures.
Bernoulli equation: transvalvular gradient (mmHg) = 4 vm squared (vm = mean velocity of blood, m/s).
Continuity equation (as printed): valve area (cm2) = SV / (ET x 85 x vm) (SV stroke volume, ET ejection time, vm mean velocity).
In aortic stenosis: mean transvalvular gradient = 2.4 vmax squared (vmax = maximum velocity of blood).
Echocardiography allows precise measurement of cardiac dimensions.
Septal and posterior wall thickness in systole and diastole allow calculation of fractional shortening and LV mass.
Fractional shortening is a crude index of LV systolic function, expressed as a percentage but not to be confused with ejection fraction.
Normal adult M-mode LV end-systolic diameter: 25-41 mm.
Normal adult M-mode LV end-diastolic diameter: 35-56 mm.
Normal aortic root diameter 20-37 mm; aortic cusp separation 15-26 mm.
Normal left atrium 19-40 mm; right ventricle 7-23 mm.
LV function can be assessed quantitatively and qualitatively.
Qualitative assessment: scoring regional wall motion and categorizing LV function as normal, mild, moderate or severe impairment.
Quantitative methods (fractional shortening, ejection fraction) are still subject to operator variability.
A nine-segment model is used for regional wall motion assessment.
Stress echo stresses the myocardium chemically or by exercise to gain information on myocardial viability and regional perfusion.
Exercise stress echo uses standard treadmill protocols such as the Bruce protocol.
Treadmill protocols give limited time to image the heart, and hyperventilation may make imaging difficult.
The main drug in pharmacological stress echo is dobutamine, in incremental low- or high-dose protocols.
Net outward systolic motion and failure of a segment to thicken in systole suggest the segment is infarcted.
Reduction of wall motion during stress in a segment that contracts at rest suggests flow-limiting coronary stenoses.
On low-dose dobutamine, improvement of a segment impaired at rest suggests stunned or hibernating myocardium.
An increase in a moderate gradient across a critically stenosed aortic valve (on stress) suggests the myocardium will respond well to valve replacement.
Papillary muscle ischemia may cause MR as a result of an inducible septal or posterior wall motion defect.
TEE has finer resolution than TTE (down to 2-3 mm).
TEE is better than TTE at imaging the posterior heart (e.g. LA appendage thrombus) and the ascending aorta.
TEE can be carried out under light sedation.
Relative contraindications to TEE: esophageal strictures (use pediatric probe), pouches and varices, respiratory compromise, cervical pathology.
TEE is told from TTE because films are usually labelled, the left atrium is closest to the transducer at the apex of the image triangle, and the AV valves are concave downwards in most views.
The apex of the TEE image is the probe in the esophagus (posterior); the left atrium is almost always at the apex of the triangle.
On TEE the right ventricle and atrium are the most anterior structures.
The aortic valve is adjacent to the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve.
In the short-axis view the inter-atrial septum points at the non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve.
In the long-axis view the aortic valve may be left or right depending on probe orientation, but is always adjacent to the interventricular septum.
TTE image quality depends on patient build (obese, emphysematous, postoperative patients are difficult), patient position, probe position and contact, and machine settings.
Failure to align the US beam parallel to blood flow underestimates its velocity and hence the transvalvular gradient.
Aligning the beam obliquely across a chamber overestimates its size.
Measuring eccentric jets or other signals instead of the main flow is an error: the MR jet may be mistaken for AS if views are poor.
A number of qualitative and quantitative variables can be used to grade regurgitation.
Mild AR: central jet width less than 25% of LVOT, regurgitant fraction less than 30%.
Moderate AR: values intermediate between mild and severe.
Severe AR: central jet width more than 65% of LVOT, regurgitant fraction more than 50%.
Mild MR: central jet less than 20% of LA area, regurgitant fraction less than 30%.
Moderate MR: values intermediate between mild and severe.
Severe MR: central jet more than 40% of LA area, regurgitant fraction more than 50%, jet impinging on the LA wall, systolic flow reversal in pulmonary veins, ERO more than 40 mm2 (printed '40mm').
Fig. 1.9 shows 9 of the 20 standard TOE views.
Mid-oesophageal views shown: four chamber, two chamber, long axis (LAX), mitral commissural, aortic valve short axis (AV SAX), bicaval.
Transgastric views shown: TG basal short axis and TG long axis.
An aortic valve long-axis view (printed 'IE AV LAX') is also shown.
Abbreviations: ME mid-oesophageal, TG transgastric, LAX long axis, SAX short axis.
The ME four-chamber view shows LA, RA, LV, RV, the tricuspid valve and mitral leaflets.
The ME long-axis view shows LA, LV, LVOT, ascending aorta, RV and mitral leaflets A2 and P2.
The ME mitral commissural view shows mitral segments P3, A2 and P1 with the LA, LV and coronary sinus.
The ME AV short-axis view shows the non-coronary (N), left (L) and right (R) coronary cusps with the LA, RA and tricuspid valve.
The ME bicaval view shows the LA, RA, SVC and IVC.
A1, A2, P1, P3 label segments of the anterior and posterior mitral leaflets.
The historic view that chronic ventricular dysfunction was synonymous with infarction was challenged in the 1970s by the observation that it could be reversed by revascularization.
'Hibernating myocardium' was coined for the theory that chronic LV dysfunction was an adaptive response to chronically reduced coronary flow at rest.
More recent studies suggest hibernation is due to repetitive stunning: adequately perfused at rest but ischemic on exercise because of impaired coronary flow reserve.
Hibernating myocardium has reduced contractility: hypokinesis rather than akinesis.
Hibernating myocardium has reduced perfusion, usually evident on exercise rather than rest.
Hibernating myocardium is viable (not infarcted), evidenced by hypokinesis.
Hibernating myocardium improves functionally with revascularization, sometimes predicted by similar improvement with inotropes or exercise (contractile reserve).
Detecting viable myocardium is clinically important in patients with poor LV function and predominantly dyspneic symptoms (rather than angina) being considered for CABG.
Absence of viability suggests much lower prognostic and symptomatic benefit from high-risk surgery.
Key modalities for assessing viability: nuclear imaging, stress echocardiography and MRI.
Nuclear imaging of the heart allows ventriculography and perfusion studies.
Isotopes may be gamma-ray or positron-emitting radionuclides.
Technetium-99m is used to make compounds such as sestamibi and tetrofosmin, which are replacing cheaper thallium-201 compounds.
These radiolabeled compounds are taken up by red blood cells (as printed).
Decay produces gamma rays which hit a sodium iodide crystal, causing scintillations detected by a photomultiplier, giving images of regional perfusion.
SPECT: two gamma cameras and computerized reconstruction allow technetium or thallium images to be reconstructed in any plane.
Stress imaging (after exercise, dobutamine, dipyridamole or adenosine) is performed first; if normal, rest imaging is not needed.
If stress imaging is abnormal, rest images are obtained: fixed perfusion defects represent infarcts, reversible defects suggest hibernation.
PET: 18F-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose (18FDG) is most widely used; it is taken up by myocytes, reflecting glucose metabolism during ischemia.
PET offers much better spatial resolution than the 1 cm of SPECT, but routine use is limited by very high costs.
Technetium-99m compounds (Table 1.4): 99mTc-labeled RBCs, 99mTc MIBI and 99mTc pyrophosphate, for blood pool studies, ventriculography and myocardial perfusion.
Thallium-201 (201TlCl) is used to image hibernation.
Nitrogen-13 is used for myocardial perfusion imaging.
An oxygen radionuclide (printed '13O') is used to image oxygen uptake.
Nuclear ventriculography provides an accurate, relatively non-invasive, reproducible ejection fraction and intracardiac shunts.
Myocardial perfusion imaging images regional blood flow after stress then at rest.
Stressors include adenosine, dobutamine (printed 'dopamine') and exercise.
During stress, territories supplied by a vessel with a flow-limiting stenosis receive relatively less blood than adjoining normal territories.
A post-stress defect that normalizes at rest (reversible defect) usually represents reversible ischemia, which may be improved by revascularization.
A photon-deficient area unchanged in both phases (fixed defect) usually represents infarction, which will not be improved by revascularization.
CMR assesses viability by end-diastolic wall thickness, dobutamine stress (contractile reserve) and contrast enhancement revealing scar tissue.
CMR also accurately measures LV and RV volumes and ejection fraction.
Late enhancement can also be shown on CT, along with wall thickness and volumes.
Fig. 1.10: thallium scan with apical perfusion defects after stress that reverse on rest images, suggesting reversible ischemia.
For emergency surgery make sure available: an ICU bed, a surgeon, anesthesiology team, an operating room, two scrub nurses, a perfusionist, blood.
Always see the patients you are operating on: take your own history and do your own examination.
Review the bloods and check that they have been cross-matched.
Review the CXR and make sure all relevant films are available.
Review echo/angiography and repeat studies more than 6 months old.
Consider whether the patient needs any additional investigations.
Decide on the order of the list with the surgeon.
Sick, complex patients who will not tolerate cancellation and would benefit from early ICU admission (full imaging and support services) are best placed first.
Patients with infection risks are placed last on the list.
The availability of equipment may dictate the running order.
Speak to the anesthesiologist, particularly if there are last-minute changes.
Make sure the nursing staff know the list order: a copy at every location with a patient on the list, ICU and OR.
When writing the list specify, besides the operation: radial artery and side, off-pump, redo, femoral bypass, thoracotomy and side.
Homografts may need to be ordered in advance.
Pacing technicians should be contacted for patients with permanent pacemakers.
Theatres should be notified of patients with latex allergies several days in advance if possible.
An outlier on a ward not used to surgery: nurses must know the patient is starved from midnight, in a gown, on a stretcher, and shaved at least 30 minutes before send time.
Let ICU know which patients are appropriate for fast-tracking.
Tell the perfusionist if the patient is anemic: they may prime the pump with blood and you will need to cross-match extra.
Tell the perfusionist if the patient weighs less than 60 kg: they may minimize prime volume to avoid hemodilution.
Tell the perfusionist if creatinine is high: they can filter the patient on bypass.
Several risk stratification tools estimate operative risk.

Most institutions submit mandatory data to registries which may publish institution- and surgeon-specific risk-adjusted outcome data (mortality and complications adjusted for comorbidities, demographics and nature of surgery).

Outcome data are usually published as raw mortality for index operations (e.g. isolated CABG) per institution or surgeon, highlighting any outside 2 standard deviations above or below the risk-adjusted mean.
Publication may have contributed to lower mortality, possibly through risk-averse behaviour leading to bias against high-risk patients.
EuroSCORE: based on European CABG patients, available as simple additive and more accurate logistic versions, tends to overestimate operative risk.
STS score: similar model validated in North American patients, freely available as an online calculator.
Parsonnet score: one of the earliest systems, not widely used now.
High-risk patients on warfarin (e.g. mechanical valve): admit early and start heparin, stopped 6 hours before surgery.
Aspirin is stopped 5 days and clopidogrel 10 days pre-op in low-risk patients.
ACE inhibitors: withhold on the day before surgery.
Non-insulin-dependent diabetics: normal medication, but withhold long-acting hypoglycaemics (gliclazide) on the morning of surgery.
Insulin-dependent diabetics should be first on the list, with morning insulin replaced by a sliding scale and iv fluids.
Obtain a carotid Doppler if there is a history of CVA, TIA or severe peripheral vascular disease.
Carotid intervention may be indicated for internal carotid stenosis more than 70%, especially if the contralateral side is tightly stenosed, to reduce the risk of CVA.
With carotid disease, discuss with a vascular surgeon and maintain high perfusion pressures.
Murmurs: all patients should have a recent pre-op TTE, and it must be reviewed.
Unexplained anemia requires full outpatient investigation.
In anemia the surgeon may prime the pump with blood rather than crystalloid; patients are not normally transfused preoperatively.
Neutrophilia: valve patients should be cancelled and a source of infection found and treated.
Neutrophilia: CABG may go ahead if WCC less than 12.0 and CRP normal; always discuss with the surgical team.
Respiratory impairment: admit high-risk patients for physiotherapy, nebulizers and education.
Renal impairment: treat acute deterioration before surgery, stop nephrotoxic drugs including ACE inhibitors, consider iv fluids.
MRSA should be treated preoperatively, consulting the infection control team.
Lung lesions should be investigated preoperatively with a lateral film and CT.
Isolated lung lesions of non-infective origin are not usually a contraindication to coronary artery surgery.

cards.q: What are the three main aims of a cardiovascular history?
cards.a: Establish the indications for surgery; identify issues needing management outside standard protocols; define the preoperative risk estimate (mortality, stroke).

importance.why: frames every pre-op clerking and links the history to risk; organizing, not life-saving

cards.q: Angina is often not classic central crushing pain. How else may it present?
cards.a: Heaviness, indigestion, isolated arm, neck or jaw discomfort, nausea, or fatigue.
points: isolated arm, neck or jaw discomfort

importance.why: atypical angina is common and easily missed; a history-taking detail

cards.q: What precipitating and relieving factors do you ask about in angina?
cards.a: Precipitants: exertion, stress, emotion, cold air. Relief: rest and sublingual nitroglycerine, and how many times a day NTG spray is used.

importance.why: history-taking detail; NTG use only informs severity

cards.q: Which functional classes of angina or dyspnea are associated with increased surgical risk?
cards.a: Class III and IV symptoms (heart failure).

importance.why: symptom class feeds every risk estimate and the consent

cards.q: How do you grade exertional dyspnea, and how is heart failure defined on that scale?
cards.a: Classify it on the NYHA scale; heart failure is defined as class III or IV symptoms.
points: heart failure is class III or IV

importance.why: the working definition of heart failure used in every assessment

cards.q: Apart from exertion, what precipitants of breathlessness do you ask about?
cards.a: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, palpitations, chest infections, COPD, pulmonary embolism, medication such as beta-blockers.

importance.why: history-taking detail

cards.q: What associated symptoms and relieving factors of breathlessness do you ask about?
cards.a: Associated: peripheral edema, palpitations, wheeze, sputum. Relieving: NTG, rest, sitting up.
points: relieved by NTG, rest, sitting up

importance.why: history-taking detail

cards.q: What do you document about a previous myocardial infarction, and how do you confirm it?
cards.a: Number, dates and anatomy of previous MIs; check the chart and the EKG for Q waves.

importance.why: documentation step; the timing card carries the decision

cards.q: How does operative risk compare after a recent STEMI versus an NSTEMI?
cards.a: Risk of surgery is higher after a recent STEMI than after an NSTEMI.

importance.why: the type of recent infarct shapes the risk and timing of CABG

cards.q: A patient needs bypass surgery three days after an MI. How does the timing affect operative risk?
cards.a: Risk is highest early after MI and falls after 1 week.

importance.why: timing of surgery after MI drives operative risk; a key viva number

cards.q: How do you establish whether a patient has had previous chest surgery?
cards.a: Ask, check the chart, and look carefully at the whole chest and back for scars.
points: look at whole chest and back for scars

importance.why: a missed previous sternotomy or thoracotomy changes the whole operative approach

cards.q: What does previous cardiac surgery mean for operative mortality and approach?
cards.a: Incremental operative mortality, and several changes to the standard operative approach.
points: changes to the standard operative approach

importance.why: redo surgery raises mortality and changes the operation; a common viva theme

cards.q: A patient is listed for redo cardiac surgery. What imaging do you request, and what does it show?
cards.a: CT chest with iv contrast: relationship of the aorta and right ventricle to the sternum, and location of patent bypass grafts.
points: aorta and right ventricle relative to sternum

importance.why: re-entry injury to the aorta, right ventricle or a patent graft can be fatal; a classic redo question

cards.q: Besides imaging, what document do you obtain before redo cardiac surgery?
cards.a: The operative report of the previous surgery.

importance.why: tells you what was done before, so the redo can be planned

cards.q: Classify angina on the Canadian Cardiovascular Society scale.
cards.a: I: no angina with ordinary activity; II: slight limitation of ordinary activity; III: marked limitation; IV: angina on minimal exertion or at rest.
points: I: no angina with ordinary activity
IV: minimal exertion or at rest

importance.why: named classification used for every coronary patient and in risk scoring; a viva classic

cards.q: Classify functional status on the New York Heart Association scale.
cards.a: I: no limitation (asymptomatic); II: slight limitation during ordinary activity; III: marked limitation of ordinary activity; IV: no physical activity without symptoms.

importance.why: named classification used for every cardiac patient and in risk scoring; a viva classic

cards.q: What does the CCS classification apply to, compared with the NYHA classification?
cards.a: CCS applies to angina only; NYHA to dyspnea and/or angina.

importance.why: distinguishes the two scales; examiners like the contrast

cards.q: A patient's breathlessness causes marked limitation of ordinary activity. What NYHA class is this, and what does it signify?
cards.a: NYHA class III: it counts as heart failure and is associated with increased surgical risk.

importance.why: applying the class to a patient is how it is used and examined

cards.q: What do you document about previous percutaneous coronary interventions?
cards.a: LV function and coronary anatomy from the angiography report; number, dates, type and result of angioplasty or stenting.

importance.why: documentation detail

cards.q: What is the operative risk of emergency surgery after a failed percutaneous coronary intervention?
cards.a: Emergency surgery after failed PCI is high risk.

importance.why: emergency surgery after failed PCI carries high risk; informs consent and planning

cards.q: A patient had a recent PCI. What antiplatelet therapy does it usually mandate, and what is the surgical impact?
cards.a: At least 1 month of clopidogrel; it can impact the conduct of coronary bypass surgery.

importance.why: antiplatelets after recent PCI shape timing and bleeding at CABG; a frequent viva question

cards.q: What non-cardiac causes of 'black-outs' should you consider?
cards.a: Epilepsy, TIAs, hypoglycemia, and vasovagal syndromes (standing, emotion, coughing, micturition).

importance.why: differential diagnosis of syncope; background

cards.q: A patient with aortic stenosis reports syncope. When does true cardiac syncope from aortic stenosis typically occur?
cards.a: On exertion: true cardiac syncope from aortic stenosis is usually exertional.

importance.why: exertional syncope in aortic stenosis is a red-flag symptom that drives valve surgery

cards.q: What does syncope while the patient is sitting or lying suggest?
cards.a: Arrhythmias.

importance.why: points to an arrhythmic cause that needs work-up

cards.q: How specific is dizziness, and what are its common drug causes?
cards.a: Fairly non-specific (may be presyncopal); common causes are antianginals, antihypertensives and diuretics causing postural hypotension.

importance.why: history detail; drugs are a reversible cause

cards.q: Apart from drugs, what may dizziness reflect?
cards.a: Low cardiac output states (failure, arrhythmias, ischemia), cerebrovascular disease, and diabetic autonomic neuropathy, probably under-recognized.
points: low cardiac output: failure, arrhythmias, ischemia

importance.why: background differential

cards.q: What may a patient mean by palpitations?
cards.a: Skipped beats, tachycardia, irregular rhythm, or awareness of their heart, particularly at night.
points: awareness of the heart at night

importance.why: history detail

cards.q: How does the onset and offset of palpitations help the diagnosis?
cards.a: Rapid onset and offset suggests paroxysmal arrhythmia; gradual onset and offset suggests sinus tachycardia.

importance.why: a simple discriminator in the history

cards.q: A patient listed for cardiac surgery is in atrial fibrillation. What may this require?
cards.a: Ablation and/or left atrial appendage ligation, and warfarin.

importance.why: adds a concomitant procedure and an anticoagulation plan

cards.q: What is the significance of peripheral edema in the cardiovascular history?
cards.a: It may go with diuretic changes, weight gain and worsening dyspnea, and helps quantify the heart failure.

importance.why: history detail that grades heart failure

cards.q: What do you ask about specifically when assessing extracardiac arteriopathy?
cards.a: TIAs, strokes, claudication, and vascular interventions.

importance.why: screens for vascular disease that alters risk and the operation

cards.q: A patient awaiting cardiac surgery gives a history of TIAs. What investigation do you request, and why?
cards.a: Carotid duplex, to exclude carotid disease, which may be an indication for carotid intervention.

importance.why: carotid disease changes the plan and the stroke risk; a classic pre-op viva question

cards.q: Why is extracardiac arteriopathy important for risk assessment and consent?
cards.a: It is important for risk scoring and affects the risk of stroke and limb ischemia quoted at consent.
points: limb ischemia risk quoted at consent

importance.why: feeds the risk score and the consent conversation

cards.q: How does extracardiac arteriopathy influence the conduct of the operation?
cards.a: It influences the choice of conduit and the cannulation site.

importance.why: the wrong conduit or cannulation site in arteriopathy causes limb ischemia or stroke

cards.q: Which reversible coronary risk factors should be addressed in hospital?
cards.a: Smoking, hypercholesterolemia, obesity, hypertension, and diabetes.

importance.why: secondary prevention in every coronary patient

cards.q: What are the irreversible coronary risk factors?
cards.a: Male sex, age, and family history.

importance.why: background

cards.q: How precisely should you record a smoking history?
cards.a: Precisely: 'non-smoker' is not the same as 'smoked 60 a day, gave up 2 weeks ago'.
points: a recent heavy ex-smoker is not a non-smoker

importance.why: history-taking detail

cards.q: In a valve patient, what do you note from the echo?
cards.a: Type and degree of valve disease, and LV function.

importance.why: the echo findings define the valve operation

cards.q: What specific past history do you ask a valve patient about?
cards.a: Rheumatic disease and endocarditis.

importance.why: history detail pointing to the valve pathology

cards.q: Before valve replacement, what must you check regarding infection?
cards.a: Recent dental clearance (not needed if edentulous) and no active sources of infection.

importance.why: an infection source can seed the new prosthesis; dental clearance is a classic pre-valve check

cards.q: Which valve patients need a preoperative coronary angiogram?
cards.a: Males over 45 years, postmenopausal females, and those with angina-type symptoms or multiple coronary risk factors.

importance.why: missed coronary disease means the wrong operation; a classic indication question

cards.q: What must you check has been discussed with a valve patient before surgery?
cards.a: The type of valve replacement.

importance.why: the choice of prosthesis must be agreed before surgery

cards.q: What are the main aims of the systems enquiry?
cards.a: Identify problems that alter standard perioperative management, contraindications to elective surgery, and problems that could delay discharge.

importance.why: frames the pre-op review of every patient

cards.q: How do you make sure the previous medical history is complete?
cards.a: Ask about other problems, then about any hospital admissions not for the heart and any operations ever; be persistent.
points: hospital admissions other than the heart

importance.why: history-taking technique

cards.q: A patient had previous chest radiotherapy. What investigation is mandatory, and why?
cards.a: A CT scan, because the aorta may be calcified.

importance.why: an unsuspected calcified aorta changes cannulation and clamping and risks stroke

cards.q: A patient for cardiac surgery has malignant disease. How does it affect the decision to operate?
cards.a: Evaluate it carefully: in most cases metastatic spread is a relative contraindication to cardiac surgery.

importance.why: decides whether to operate at all

cards.q: Why does thyroid disease matter perioperatively?
cards.a: It may dictate the choice of antiarrhythmic.

importance.why: a niche drug-choice point

cards.q: How should a patient with a hip replacement be transferred, and why?
cards.a: With a pillow between the legs: adducting the hip may cause dislocation.

importance.why: a handling detail; harm is avoidable but not life-threatening

cards.q: A patient has thrombocytopenia, a factor deficiency or a thrombophilia. What do you arrange before surgery?
cards.a: Review by a hematologist.

importance.why: bleeding or clotting disorders cause major perioperative complications

cards.q: Which allergies must you specifically ask about, and what drug details do you take?
cards.a: Allergies to drugs, iodine, contrast and fish; full details of all drugs, doses and regimens.

importance.why: a missed allergy can cause a serious reaction in theatre

cards.q: Why does a fish allergy matter in cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Protamine is made from salmon sperm.

importance.why: a protamine reaction at heparin reversal can be catastrophic

cards.q: A patient has a latex allergy. What must you do?
cards.a: Warn the operating room: latex allergy requires changes to equipment.

importance.why: latex exposure in theatre can cause a severe reaction

cards.q: A patient has a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. How does this affect cardiopulmonary bypass?
cards.a: Non-heparin bypass (bivalirudin or argatroban) may be required, which mandates careful preplanning.

importance.why: heparin re-exposure in HIT can be catastrophic; a classic viva scenario

cards.q: How do you manage antianginal drugs around surgery?
cards.a: Continue them until surgery, and stop them postoperatively.

importance.why: routine drug plan for every coronary patient

cards.q: How do you manage beta-blockers around surgery?
cards.a: Continue them until surgery; reintroduce them postoperatively as blood pressure and rhythm permit.
points: as blood pressure and rhythm permit

importance.why: daily drug plan, commonly asked

cards.q: When do you stop ACE inhibitors before cardiac surgery, and why?
cards.a: 24 to 48 hours before surgery, to avoid profound peripheral dilatation in the immediate postoperative period.

importance.why: postoperative vasodilatation is common and dangerous; a key pre-op number

cards.q: When, and why, do many surgeons stop aspirin and clopidogrel before surgery?
cards.a: 5 to 10 days preoperatively, because they predispose to increased postoperative bleeding.

importance.why: antiplatelet timing is daily practice and a frequent viva question

cards.q: What is the downside of stopping aspirin and clopidogrel before surgery?
cards.a: A slightly higher risk of acute ischemic events.

importance.why: the bleeding-versus-ischemia trade-off behind the antiplatelet decision

cards.q: A patient with a tight left main stem is on aspirin and clopidogrel. Do you stop them before surgery?
cards.a: They may be continued in high-risk patients, such as tight left main stem or recent PCI.

importance.why: stopping antiplatelets in high-risk coronary anatomy risks infarction before surgery

cards.q: When should warfarin be stopped before surgery?
cards.a: 5 days before surgery.

importance.why: bleeding risk if warfarin is not stopped in time

cards.q: A patient on warfarin has had a previous DVT. How do you manage anticoagulation before surgery?
cards.a: Stop warfarin 5 days before, and admit 24 to 48 hours pre-op for iv heparin.

importance.why: thromboembolic risk while off warfarin in high-risk patients

cards.q: In general, what should be done with steroid doses before surgery?
cards.a: Reduce them where possible.

importance.why: a general principle; the cover card carries the danger

cards.q: A patient takes more than 5 mg of prednisone daily. What steroid cover do you prescribe?
cards.a: Hydrocortisone 50 to 100 mg iv 6-hourly, or an equivalent infusion, for 48 hours, starting with the premedication.

importance.why: missed steroid cover causes Addisonian crisis, which can kill

cards.q: What complication does perioperative steroid cover prevent, and by what mechanism?
cards.a: Addisonian crisis, as a result of adrenal suppression.

importance.why: explains why steroid cover is given

cards.q: How do you manage diabetic medication on the morning of surgery?
cards.a: Withhold long-acting hypoglycemics and commence an insulin sliding scale where appropriate.

importance.why: perioperative hypoglycemia is avoidable harm in a common patient group

cards.q: What may a Jehovah's witness patient refuse in cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Blood and blood products; some may not agree to the use of cell salvage.

importance.why: shapes the whole blood conservation plan

cards.q: A Jehovah's witness needs cardiac surgery. What must happen preoperatively?
cards.a: Identify them preoperatively, counsel them, and clearly document their preferences.

importance.why: bleeding without agreed blood products can be fatal; must be settled before surgery

cards.q: What preoperative hematocrit do you aim for in a Jehovah's witness, and how may you achieve it?
cards.a: More than 40%; several weeks of erythropoietin therapy may be indicated.

importance.why: a key number for bloodless surgery

cards.q: Which patients are at risk of alcohol withdrawal?
cards.a: Heavy or binge drinkers.

importance.why: unrecognized withdrawal causes avoidable postoperative harm

cards.q: What are the risks of haloperidol in alcohol withdrawal?
cards.a: It lowers the seizure threshold and prolongs the QT.

importance.why: the wrong sedative can provoke seizures or arrhythmia

cards.q: What do you prescribe for alcohol withdrawal?
cards.a: Diazepam 2 mg orally 8-hourly, thiamine and folate.

importance.why: a practical prescription on the ward

cards.q: A patient lives alone. What should you plan?
cards.a: Rehabilitation.

importance.why: discharge planning

cards.q: A patient walks with a stick or frame. Why contact physiotherapists early?
cards.a: Sternal union may be compromised even if mobility is not.

importance.why: protects the sternum during rehabilitation

cards.q: A patient admitted for elective cardiac surgery has an active upper respiratory tract infection. What do you do?
cards.a: Cancel the operation: an active URTI is sufficient reason.

importance.why: operating through an active infection risks serious respiratory complications

cards.q: How do you assess a suspected upper respiratory tract infection before surgery?
cards.a: Ask about cough, colds and sputum; measure temperature, CRP and white cell count; get a chest X-ray.

importance.why: decides whether the infection is active

cards.q: How do you assess COPD in the history?
cards.a: Ask about hospital admissions, inhalers, nebulizers and home oxygen.

importance.why: grades lung disease that raises operative risk

cards.q: A patient with COPD has dyspnea as the prominent symptom. What do you request?
cards.a: Lung function tests, including blood gases.

importance.why: separates cardiac from respiratory breathlessness and grades risk

cards.q: What gastrointestinal complications are cardiac surgery patients at risk of?
cards.a: Upper GI bleeding from peptic ulcer disease, prolonged ileus, and acute deterioration of disease such as pancreatitis or cholecystitis.
points: upper GI bleed from peptic ulcer

importance.why: GI complications after cardiac surgery are serious and often asked

cards.q: Which GI problems should you ask about specifically?
cards.a: Dyspepsia, ulcers, and pancreatitis.

importance.why: history detail

cards.q: What GI prophylaxis do all cardiac surgery patients receive?
cards.a: Prophylactic proton pump inhibitors.

importance.why: routine prophylaxis against upper GI bleeding

cards.q: A patient is at risk of GI bleeding. How do you adjust analgesia and aspirin?
cards.a: Note on the drug chart to avoid NSAIDs; give aspirin enteric coated and with food.

importance.why: reduces avoidable GI bleeding

cards.q: The notes show an acute deterioration in renal function before elective surgery. What do you consider?
cards.a: Delaying the patient to optimize renal function.

importance.why: operating during acute renal deterioration risks postoperative renal failure

cards.q: How do you optimize acutely deteriorated renal function before surgery?
cards.a: Stop nephrotoxic drugs including ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs, start iv fluids with careful fluid balance, and in some cases dialysis.
points: iv fluids with careful fluid balance

importance.why: practical renal optimization before surgery

cards.q: When should a dialysis patient be dialysed before cardiac surgery?
cards.a: The morning of surgery or the night before.

importance.why: fluid and potassium control at the start of surgery

cards.q: Why are patients undergoing preoperative cardiac catheterization at risk of renal impairment?
cards.a: Hypovolemia from preprocedure fasting combined with nephrotoxic contrast.

importance.why: common, preventable renal insult before surgery

cards.q: How do you protect borderline renal function before contrast studies?
cards.a: Prescribe iv fluid, and consider iv acetylcysteine.

importance.why: prevents contrast nephropathy before surgery

cards.q: A patient has symptoms of prostatic enlargement. What should you warn him about?
cards.a: He may need a suprapubic catheter.

importance.why: a consent detail

cards.q: What do you identify in the neurological history?
cards.a: TIAs, strokes, residual deficit, and dementia.

importance.why: baseline neurology for stroke risk and consent

cards.q: Is dementia a contraindication to cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Advanced dementia is a contraindication to cardiac surgery.

importance.why: decides whether to operate

cards.q: What are the main purposes of the preoperative examination?
cards.a: Identify disease needing further investigation and management, help plan surgery, and identify problems that may delay recovery.

importance.why: frames the examination of every patient

cards.q: Does the average elective patient need the full cardiovascular examination?
cards.a: No: a shortened version of the full examination is sufficient.

importance.why: practical point about routine practice

cards.q: What does the short preoperative examination include?
cards.a: Pulse, BP, JVP at 45 degrees, heart, carotids and breath sounds, scars, abdomen, peripheral pulses with aorta, pedal edema, conduits.
points: abdomen; peripheral pulses and abdominal aorta

importance.why: the routine examination done on every elective patient

cards.q: At what position do you assess the jugular venous pressure?
cards.a: With the patient at 45 degrees.

importance.why: basic examination technique

cards.q: What do you assess at general inspection from the end of the bed?
cards.a: Comfort at rest, need for oxygen, well or moribund, obese or cachexic, and features of Down's or Marfan syndrome.

importance.why: a quick global assessment of every patient

cards.q: What cardiac lesions do features of Down's syndrome and of Marfan syndrome suggest?
cards.a: Down's: atrial or ventricular septal defect. Marfan: aortic aneurysms, dissection and incompetence.

importance.why: syndromic features point to serious structural disease

cards.q: What do you look for in the hands and forearms?
cards.a: Nicotine staining, tendon xanthoma, and stigmata of endocarditis: splinter hemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, petechiae.

importance.why: endocarditis stigmata change the timing and type of valve surgery

cards.q: What are Osler's nodes, and how do they differ from Janeway lesions?
