cards.a: Osler's nodes: tender lumps in the fingertip pulps. Janeway lesions: red macules on the palms or flexor aspects of the wrist.
points: Janeway: red macules, palms or flexor wrist

importance.why: classic signs of endocarditis; descriptive

cards.q: Where do you assess the rate, rhythm, character and volume of the pulse?
cards.a: Rate and rhythm at the radial; character and volume at the brachial or carotid; also feel peripheral pulses and the abdominal aorta.
points: character and volume: brachial or carotid

importance.why: basic examination technique

cards.q: Contrast the pulse of aortic stenosis with that of aortic incompetence.
cards.a: Aortic stenosis: slow rising, thready pulse. Aortic incompetence: large volume, bounding pulse.

importance.why: classic bedside signs of the two commonest aortic valve lesions

cards.q: Preoperatively a patient's systolic pressure is more than 180 mmHg. How do you treat it?
cards.a: Nifedipine 10 mg sublingually preoperatively.

importance.why: uncontrolled hypertension at induction is avoidable harm

cards.q: What does a wide pulse pressure suggest?
cards.a: Aortic incompetence.

importance.why: a classic sign of aortic incompetence

cards.q: How do you measure blood pressure in a patient with fat arms, and why?
cards.a: Use a broad cuff, as BP will otherwise be underestimated.

importance.why: measurement technique

cards.q: You suspect aortic dissection or coarctation. How do you measure the blood pressure?
cards.a: In both arms.

importance.why: a simple bedside clue to dissection or coarctation

cards.q: What is malar flush, and which valve lesion is it characteristic of?
cards.a: Cyanosis in a butterfly rash distribution; characteristic of mitral stenosis.

importance.why: a classic but uncommon sign

cards.q: A patient with a prosthetic heart valve is jaundiced. What may be the cause?
cards.a: Hemolysis from the prosthetic heart valve.

importance.why: hemolysis can signal a failing prosthesis that needs reoperation

cards.q: What do xanthelasma and corneal arcus indicate?
cards.a: Hyperlipidemia: they are common signs of it.

importance.why: background sign of a risk factor

cards.q: What eye signs may suggest infective endocarditis, and syphilitic aortic incompetence?
cards.a: Roth spots in infective endocarditis; Argyll Robertson pupils, rarely, in syphilitic aortic incompetence.
points: Argyll Robertson pupils: syphilitic aortic incompetence

importance.why: uncommon eye signs

cards.q: What do you look for in the mouth of a cardiac surgical patient?
cards.a: Central cyanosis on the tongue and gums, the high arched palate of Marfan, and poor dentition, particularly in valve patients.

importance.why: a quick screen for cyanosis, Marfan and a dental infection source

cards.q: What do you inspect the chest for, and why expose it fully?
cards.a: Scars (lateral thoracotomies, median sternotomy), ICD or pacemaker, pectus, visible pulsations; without exposure you will miss them.

importance.why: a missed scar or device changes the operative approach

cards.q: Define the apex beat and give its normal position.
cards.a: The point furthest from the manubrium where the heart can be felt; normally the 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line.
points: furthest point from manubrium where heart is felt

importance.why: basic sign that other apex findings build on

cards.q: What does a laterally displaced apex beat indicate?
cards.a: Cardiomegaly or mediastinal shift.

importance.why: a common sign; informs, rarely decides

cards.q: What causes a sustained, forceful apex beat?
cards.a: Aortic stenosis and hypertensive cardiomyopathy.

importance.why: bedside sign of pressure-loaded LV

cards.q: How is the apex beat altered in aortic regurgitation and in mitral stenosis?
cards.a: Aortic regurgitation (dilated LV): displaced downwards. Mitral stenosis: tapping.

importance.why: classic valve signs

cards.q: What does a left parasternal heave indicate, and what is a thrill?
cards.a: A heave suggests right ventricular hypertrophy; a thrill is a palpable murmur.

importance.why: basic palpation findings

cards.q: How do you time heart sounds, and when do you use the bell versus the diaphragm?
cards.a: Time them against the radial pulse; bell for low-pitched sounds, diaphragm for high-pitched sounds.

importance.why: basic auscultation technique

cards.q: Where do you auscultate the heart?
cards.a: Apex (diaphragm and bell), upper and lower left sternal borders, under the clavicles, over the carotids, and in the axilla.
points: upper and lower left sternal borders

importance.why: basic auscultation technique

cards.q: After the standard sites, in which two positions do you listen again?
cards.a: At the apex in the left lateral position; at the lower left sternal border sitting forward in full expiration.
points: lower left sternal border, sitting forward

importance.why: standard manoeuvres to bring out murmurs

cards.q: How are murmurs graded, and what defines grade 1?
cards.a: On a scale of 1 to 6; grade 1 is just audible in a quiet room with the patient breath holding.
points: grade 1: just audible in a quiet room

importance.why: a standard grading scale

cards.q: On the murmur grading scale, what defines grade 3 and grade 6?
cards.a: Grade 3: easy to hear, without a thrill. Grade 6: audible without a stethoscope.
points: grade 3: easy to hear, no thrill

importance.why: a standard grading scale

cards.q: On examination you hear a murmur or a carotid bruit. What do you do next?
cards.a: Arrange ultrasound imaging.

importance.why: an undiagnosed valve lesion or carotid stenosis changes the operation

cards.q: List the causes of an ejection systolic murmur.
cards.a: Aortic stenosis, aortic sclerosis, pulmonary stenosis, ASD, and innocent flow murmur from anemia, hyperthyroidism or pregnancy.
points: innocent flow murmur: anemia, hyperthyroid, pregnancy

importance.why: a classic murmur differential

cards.q: Describe the murmur of aortic stenosis.
cards.a: Ejection systolic, loudest in the aortic area in expiration, radiating to the carotids.
points: loudest in aortic area in expiration

importance.why: the commonest valve lesion operated on; a classic sign

cards.q: List the causes of a pansystolic murmur.
cards.a: Mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation, VSD, and patent ductus arteriosus.

importance.why: a classic murmur differential

cards.q: Describe the murmur of mitral regurgitation.
cards.a: Pansystolic, loudest at the apex, radiating to the axilla.

importance.why: a common operated lesion; a classic sign

cards.q: What causes early diastolic and mid diastolic murmurs?
cards.a: Early diastolic: aortic and pulmonary regurgitation. Mid diastolic: mitral stenosis, tricuspid stenosis, Austin Flint murmur of aortic regurgitation.
points: Austin Flint murmur of aortic regurgitation

importance.why: a classic murmur differential

cards.q: How do you examine the legs for vein conduit?
cards.a: Stand the patient up to see both legs from ankle to groin; look for varicosities and whether they are long or short saphenous.

importance.why: conduit assessment for every CABG

cards.q: What is Allen's test for, and how do you perform it?
cards.a: Radial artery suitability: patient clenches fist, occlude radial and ulnar pulses, hand opened, release ulnar, time the palm pinking up.
points: clench fist, occlude radial and ulnar

importance.why: a classic bedside test before radial harvest

cards.q: On Allen's test, what refill time makes the radial artery suitable for harvest?
cards.a: A refill time of less than 5 seconds.

importance.why: harvesting a radial without adequate ulnar supply risks hand ischemia; a key number

cards.q: What does the general examination consist of?
cards.a: Listen to the chest and palpate the abdomen.

importance.why: routine step

cards.q: Apart from the cross-match, which routine blood tests do you send before surgery?
cards.a: CBC; coagulation screen (APTT and PT, INR if on warfarin); Chem 7 biochemistry; liver function tests.

importance.why: every patient gets them; the baseline the rest of the work-up builds on

cards.q: What does the Chem 7 biochemistry panel contain?
cards.a: Sodium; potassium; chloride; bicarbonate; blood urea nitrogen; creatinine; glucose.

importance.why: routine panel; background knowledge rarely asked on its own

cards.q: How many units of blood do you routinely cross-match before surgery?
cards.a: 2 units.

importance.why: routine blood preparation for every case

cards.q: A patient is listed for a reoperation or a thoracoabdominal repair: what blood do you cross-match?
cards.a: 4 units plus fresh frozen plasma and platelets.

importance.why: massive bleeding at re-entry or thoracoabdominal repair without blood ready can be fatal

cards.q: Apart from blood tests, what screening is routine before surgery?
cards.a: MRSA screening swab; urinalysis; pregnancy test; sickle cell testing.

importance.why: routine screening for every patient; MRSA status matters for wound and valve infection

cards.q: What causes a sodium above 145 millimoles per litre?
cards.a: Commonly diarrhea and vomiting; less commonly diabetes insipidus.

importance.why: uncommon preoperative finding; background medicine

cards.q: How do you manage hypernatremia found before surgery?
cards.a: Oral water or intravenous 5 percent dextrose; discuss with the anesthesiologist.

importance.why: simple correction; rarely decisive for surgery

cards.q: What are the common causes of a sodium below 130 millimoles per litre?
cards.a: Diuretics, diarrhea and vomiting.

importance.why: diuretic-induced hyponatremia is regular in cardiac patients

cards.q: What are the less common causes of hyponatremia, and which is common after surgery?
cards.a: Congestive cardiac failure, cirrhosis, renal failure; Addison's; SIADH, which is common postoperatively.

importance.why: postoperative SIADH is a common cause of low sodium on the ward

cards.q: A patient has a sodium below 130 before surgery: how do you manage it?
cards.a: Assess renal function and treat accordingly; fluid restrict if appropriate; discuss with the anesthesiologist.

importance.why: uncorrected hyponatremia raises perioperative risk; management depends on renal function

cards.q: What are the common causes of a potassium above 5 millimoles per litre?
cards.a: Potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE inhibitors; excess potassium therapy; artifact from hemolysis in the tube.

importance.why: cardiac patients are on these drugs; hyperkalemia causes arrhythmia

cards.q: What are the less common causes of hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Renal failure; diabetic acidosis; Addison's disease.

importance.why: less common causes; background medicine

cards.q: A well patient's potassium comes back above 5: what simple cause must you exclude?
cards.a: Artifact: hemolysis in the tube.

importance.why: a spurious result can cancel or wrongly treat a patient; check the sample first

cards.q: Over what time should preoperative hyperkalemia or hypokalemia be correctable?
cards.a: Over 12 hours.

importance.why: potassium is corrected in every cardiac patient; tells you whether to delay the list

cards.q: What causes a potassium below 3.5 millimoles per litre?
cards.a: Commonly diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea; less commonly Conn's, Cushing's syndromes, renal tubular failure.

importance.why: diuretic hypokalemia is everyday in cardiac patients and provokes arrhythmia

cards.q: Above what creatinine and BUN levels do you call it renal impairment?
cards.a: Creatinine more than 1.2 mg/dL; BUN more than 21 mg/dL.

importance.why: renal impairment raises operative risk and changes perioperative care

cards.q: What does a disproportionately raised urea suggest?
cards.a: Dehydration as the primary cause.

importance.why: classic interpretation of the urea to creatinine pattern

cards.q: What causes an isolated rise in urea?
cards.a: Thiazide diuretics; gout; lymphoma; leukemia.

importance.why: a rarity of the biochemistry table; background only

cards.q: Which drugs commonly cause raised liver function tests?
cards.a: Paracetamol; oral contraceptive pill; co-amoxiclav; chlorpromazine; erythromycin.

importance.why: general medicine background

cards.q: Apart from drugs, what causes raised liver function tests or bilirubin?
cards.a: Hemolysis; viral hepatitis; gallstones; Gilbert's syndrome; sepsis; alcohol; less commonly malignant biliary obstruction.

importance.why: deranged LFTs are met often; liver disease adds operative risk

cards.q: How do you assess a patient with raised liver function tests at the bedside?
cards.a: Ask about iv drug use, transfusions, travel, alcohol; examine for big liver or spleen and chronic liver disease.

importance.why: standard work-up; rarely decisive

cards.q: Which investigations do you request for unexplained raised LFTs?
cards.a: Urine for bilirubin and urobilinogen; liver ultrasound; consider serology.

importance.why: finding liver disease changes operative risk

cards.q: On what basis do you cancel surgery because of an abnormal preoperative screening result?
cards.a: Weigh the risk of delaying surgery against the increased risk of surgery; discuss any cancellation with the surgical team.

importance.why: decides whether to operate today; a core judgement examiners probe

cards.q: An unstable patient with a tight left main stem lesion has a mild neutrophilia: do you cancel?
cards.a: Less likely than an elective valve patient: weigh the risk of delay against surgical risk; discuss with the team.

importance.why: cancelling an unstable left main patient for a trivial result can kill

cards.q: Hemoglobin is below 9.5 with an MCV below 75: what are the causes?
cards.a: Iron deficiency; thalassemia.

importance.why: classic MCV-based classification of anemia

cards.q: What causes anemia with an MCV of 75 to 95?
cards.a: Chronic disease; renal failure; bone marrow failure; hemolysis; hypothyroidism; acute dilution.

importance.why: medical classification; background for the surgeon

cards.q: What causes anemia with an MCV above 95?
cards.a: Low B12 or folate; alcohol; liver disease; hypothyroidism; myelodysplasias; bone marrow infiltration.

importance.why: medical classification; background for the surgeon

cards.q: A patient awaiting cardiac surgery has undiagnosed iron deficiency anemia: what must you do?
cards.a: Investigate fully: GI malignancy is a common cause in this age group.

importance.why: a missed GI cancer changes the plan and the prognosis

cards.q: How do you manage a low preoperative hemoglobin regarding transfusion?
cards.a: Treat the cause where possible; avoid transfusion unless the hemoglobin is very low.

importance.why: blood conservation applies to every cardiac patient

cards.q: Why might the perfusionist ask for extra blood for an anemic patient?
cards.a: To prime the pump.

importance.why: links preoperative anemia to bypass planning

cards.q: Hemoglobin is above 14: what is relative versus absolute polycythemia?
cards.a: Relative: reduced plasma volume from dehydration (alcohol, diuretics); absolute: raised red cell mass.

importance.why: uncommon finding; background classification

cards.q: What causes an absolute polycythemia?
cards.a: Primary polycythemia rubra vera; secondary to smoking, COPD, altitude, tumours.

importance.why: smokers with COPD are common in thoracic practice

cards.q: A patient with polycythemia rubra vera has surgery: what postoperative risk, and how do you prevent it?
cards.a: Thromboembolic events; may need formal anticoagulation postoperatively.

importance.why: a postoperative thrombosis is a preventable complication

cards.q: What causes a neutrophilia?
cards.a: Bacterial sepsis; trauma; surgery; burns; inflammation; MI; polymyalgia; steroids; hemorrhage.

importance.why: a raised white count is common; sepsis must be separated from benign causes

cards.q: What causes a lymphocytosis, and what causes an eosinophilia?
cards.a: Lymphocytosis: viral infection (EBV, CMV), CLL. Eosinophilia: asthma, allergy, parasites, eczema, malignancy.

importance.why: general medicine background

cards.q: A preoperative patient has a white count above 12: how do you assess them?
cards.a: Recheck history and examination for sepsis; take the temperature; look at the CXR and urine dipsticks.

importance.why: occult sepsis must be found before an implant goes in

cards.q: An elective valve patient has a raised white count: what do you do?
cards.a: Check with the team: surgery may be cancelled.

importance.why: operating with occult sepsis risks prosthetic infection; a cancel-or-proceed decision

cards.q: The raised white count is from an upper respiratory tract infection: how do you manage it?
cards.a: Start antibiotics and recheck the white count in 2 to 3 weeks.

importance.why: sets the timing of elective surgery

cards.q: What causes a white count below 2?
cards.a: Rarely neutropenic sepsis; steroids; sulfonamides; SLE.

importance.why: rare finding; background

cards.q: A patient has a white count below 2 and is septic: what do you do?
cards.a: Discuss with a hematologist: it is an emergency in sepsis.

importance.why: neutropenic sepsis is an emergency that can kill

cards.q: What causes a platelet count above 400?
cards.a: Essential thrombocythemia; sepsis; inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis.

importance.why: uncommon finding; background

cards.q: What proportion of patients with a raised platelet count have malignancy, and who do you involve?
cards.a: 50 percent; discuss with a hematologist.

importance.why: a number to know but rarely decisive for surgery

cards.q: What causes a platelet count below 120?
cards.a: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; sepsis and DIC; drugs; SLE; lymphoma; bone marrow failure.

importance.why: low platelets raise bleeding risk and may signal HIT

cards.q: A patient on heparin has a platelet count below 120: what do you do?
cards.a: Discontinue heparin and request a heparin-induced thrombocytopenia screen.

importance.why: missed HIT before heparinisation for bypass can cause catastrophic thrombosis

cards.q: A septic patient has a low platelet count: what do you send?
cards.a: Fibrin degradation products; and request platelets.

importance.why: screens for DIC, which changes bleeding risk

cards.q: What causes a raised PT, and a raised INR?
cards.a: PT: warfarin, low vitamin K, liver disease. INR: warfarin, liver disease.

importance.why: warfarin is common in cardiac patients and must be reversed or stopped before surgery

cards.q: What causes a raised APTT?
cards.a: Heparin; low factor VIII or IX.

importance.why: heparin is given to every bypass patient; reading the APTT is daily work and alters bleeding risk

cards.q: How do you manage an unexplained clotting abnormality before surgery?
cards.a: Investigate as for liver disease; measure clotting factors; talk to a hematologist.

importance.why: an uncorrected coagulopathy means bleeding after bypass

cards.q: The blood bank reports atypical antibodies: what does that mean for your list?
cards.a: More time and further samples are needed to obtain satisfactorily cross-matched blood.

importance.why: operating before compatible blood is available risks a bleed without products

cards.q: What is the standard chest X-ray view, and how is it taken?
cards.a: Posteroanterior: patient stands facing the film, clasping it; X-rays pass back to front in full inspiration.

importance.why: basic radiograph technique every surgeon reads daily

cards.q: Why is a chest film taken in full inspiration?
cards.a: To maximize the size of the lung fields.

importance.why: technical background

cards.q: When is an AP chest film used, and how is it taken?
cards.a: Portable films in immobile patients: plate under the back, X-rays pass from front to back.

importance.why: every ICU film is AP; you must know its limits

cards.q: What are the advantages of a PA over an AP chest film?
cards.a: Scapulae rotated away; smaller heart shadow, so more lung visible; cardiomegaly and mediastinal widening reliably assessed.

importance.why: a classic short-answer on film projection

cards.q: Why be cautious calling cardiomegaly or a wide mediastinum on a portable AP film?
cards.a: The heart shadow is larger on AP; only PA proportions reliably show cardiomegaly and mediastinal widening.

importance.why: over-reading a wide mediastinum on an AP film sends patients for the wrong work-up

cards.q: What is a lateral chest film for, and how is a left lateral taken?
cards.a: To define abnormalities seen on PA or AP films; left side against the film, labelled L, for the left thorax.
points: define abnormalities seen on PA or AP

importance.why: technique detail; rarely examined

cards.q: Describe your system for presenting a chest X-ray.
cards.a: Patient details and date; film type and orientation; alignment, coverage, exposure; lines; bones; soft tissues; mediastinum; airways and lungs.

importance.why: every viva hands you a film; a systematic description is expected

cards.q: What do you check first when you are shown a chest film?
cards.a: Name, age and film date; film type (AP, PA or lateral, erect or supine, contrast or plain); orientation.
points: erect or supine; contrast or plain

importance.why: the opening of every film description

cards.q: How do you check that a chest film is correctly aligned?
cards.a: Clavicles and ribs should be symmetrically aligned with the sternum and spinous processes.

importance.why: film quality basics

cards.q: How do you judge the coverage and exposure of a chest film?
cards.a: All lung fields from apex to costophrenic angle; vertebral bodies visible through the heart.
points: vertebral bodies seen through the heart

importance.why: film quality basics

cards.q: What lines and devices do you comment on in a chest film?
cards.a: ET and NG tubes; PA catheter or central line; clips; drains; prosthetic valves; rings; wires.

importance.why: every postoperative film carries these devices

cards.q: What do you look for in the bones on a chest film, and where are ribs best seen?
cards.a: Fractures and dislocations; lytic lesions; calcification; erosions; extra ribs. Ribs are easier to see posteriorly.

importance.why: part of the routine; rarely decisive

cards.q: Which soft tissues do you assess on a chest film, and which hemidiaphragm is normally higher?
cards.a: Neck, chest wall and breasts; the right hemidiaphragm is normally one rib higher than the left.

importance.why: a raised left hemidiaphragm is abnormal; needs the normal relation

cards.q: What structures make up the mediastinal shadow on a chest film?
cards.a: Aortic knob; pulmonary trunk; left atrial appendage; left ventricle; IVC; right atrium; SVC.

importance.why: cardiac contours are the foundation of reading cardiac films

cards.q: After the mediastinum, what do you assess on a chest film?
cards.a: Airways (trachea, main bronchi), lung fields, fissures and the vascularity of the lung fields.

importance.why: part of the routine description

cards.q: How do you judge a good inspiratory chest film?
cards.a: The lungs inflate to the 10th rib posteriorly or the 6th rib anteriorly.

importance.why: a common examiner's number for film adequacy

cards.q: On a normal chest film, where should the trachea be, and how should opacities appear?
cards.a: The trachea should be midline; opacities should be symmetrical.

importance.why: tracheal deviation is the first clue to tension or collapse

cards.q: How much pleural fluid is needed to blunt the costophrenic angle?

importance.why: a classic number; a normal angle does not exclude an effusion

cards.q: How does a pleural collection appear on a supine film?
cards.a: No fluid level: it appears as a diffuse opacity.

importance.why: ICU films are supine; a hemothorax seen only as haze is easily missed

cards.q: One hemithorax is more opaque than the other: what are the two possibilities?
cards.a: A collection on the opaque side, or a pneumothorax on the other side.

importance.why: confusing the two leads to draining the wrong side

cards.q: On a PA chest film, what forms the left mediastinal border, from above down?
cards.a: Aortic knuckle; pulmonary trunk; left atrial appendage; left ventricle.

importance.why: a classic film question; contour changes point to chamber or aortic disease

cards.q: On a PA chest film, what forms the right mediastinal border?
cards.a: Superior vena cava, right atrium, and the inferior vena cava below.

importance.why: a classic film question on normal contours

cards.q: Which airway and pleural landmarks do you identify on a normal PA film?
cards.a: Trachea; carina; hemidiaphragms; costophrenic angles; lung apices.

importance.why: normal anatomy background for film reading

cards.q: Which bony landmarks would you identify on a normal PA chest film?
cards.a: Spinous processes; first rib; clavicle; body of scapula; lower ribs such as the eighth.

importance.why: normal anatomy background

cards.q: On a lateral chest film, which cardiac chambers lie anteriorly and posteriorly?
cards.a: Right ventricle anteriorly; left atrium posteriorly; left ventricle in between.

importance.why: anterior structures behind the sternum matter at resternotomy

cards.q: What great vessel and airway structures do you identify on a lateral chest film?
cards.a: Ascending aorta; distal aortic arch; pulmonary trunk; aortopulmonary window; proximal and distal trachea.

importance.why: normal lateral anatomy; the aortopulmonary window is often asked

cards.q: What bony and diaphragmatic landmarks are seen on a lateral chest film?
cards.a: Manubriosternal junction; thoracic vertebral bodies; body of scapula; right and left hemidiaphragms.

importance.why: normal anatomy background

cards.q: When is the first chest film taken after cardiac surgery?
cards.a: A portable film on immediate arrival in the ICU.

importance.why: the baseline check of every tube and line

cards.q: What lines and devices are commonly seen on an early postoperative cardiac film?
cards.a: ET tube; NG tube; PA catheter and sheath; sternal wires; EKG leads; chest tubes; prosthetic valve.

importance.why: every ICU film; the examiner points at each one

cards.q: Where should the endotracheal tube tip lie on the postoperative film?
cards.a: 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the carina.

importance.why: a malpositioned tube means one-lung ventilation or extubation risk; a classic number

cards.q: Where should the nasogastric tube be on the postoperative film?
cards.a: Visible in the stomach.

importance.why: routine line check

cards.q: Where should a PA catheter lie on the postoperative film, and what malpositions do you look for?
cards.a: Usually the right pulmonary artery; check it is not coiled, in too far, or malpositioned, e.g. in the IVC.

importance.why: a catheter in too far can injure the pulmonary artery; checked on every film

cards.q: Beyond the lines, what do you look for on the first ICU film?
cards.a: Collections, which may be only diffuse haze when supine; pneumothorax; lobar collapse.

importance.why: missed bleeding or pneumothorax after surgery is dangerous

cards.q: What is the chest X-ray appearance of a pericardial effusion?
cards.a: A globular heart shadow.

importance.why: a classic film sign that should prompt echo

cards.q: You suspect a pericardial effusion or tamponade: which tests are diagnostic?
cards.a: CT and echo diagnose an effusion; echo is required to diagnose tamponade.

importance.why: missed tamponade kills; a classic viva question

cards.q: On an erect film, what sign suggests a pleural effusion?
cards.a: A concave upwards meniscus.

importance.why: effusions are common after cardiothoracic surgery

cards.q: A pleural collection shows a flat fluid level: what does that suggest?
cards.a: A hydropneumothorax.

importance.why: air and fluid together change the drainage plan

cards.q: Which non-vascular structures do you identify on a normal contrast CT of the upper chest?
cards.a: Trachea; right and left lungs; body of T3; esophagus.

importance.why: normal cross-sectional anatomy; background

cards.q: Above the aortic arch on contrast CT, which vessels do you identify?
cards.a: SVC full of contrast; brachiocephalic artery; left common carotid; left subclavian artery.

importance.why: arch vessel anatomy underpins dissection and arch surgery

cards.q: Moving down from the aortic arch on contrast CT, what do you identify at the pulmonary trunk level?
cards.a: Ascending aorta; pulmonary trunk; descending aorta; carina.

importance.why: you must find the ascending and descending aorta to read a dissection CT

cards.q: On axial contrast CT at the level of the heart, what structures do you identify?
cards.a: Right ventricle anteriorly; right atrium; left atrium posteriorly; hemiazygous vein.

importance.why: normal cross-sectional anatomy

cards.q: On contrast CT for suspected type A dissection, what do you look for, and how may it appear?
cards.a: A dissection flap; often less prominent and more concave than an obvious one.

importance.why: a missed type A dissection kills; subtle flaps are the trap

cards.q: How does CT differ from a standard X-ray?
cards.a: Same radiation as standard X-rays, but the X-ray source moves round the patient.

importance.why: basic imaging physics; background only

cards.q: What is the Hounsfield scale, and what values mark water, white and black?
cards.a: Scale of attenuation: water 0 HU, ranging from plus 1000 (white) to minus 1000 (black).

importance.why: underpins reading every CT; rarely asked in a surgical viva

cards.q: Give the Hounsfield values of bone, contrast, soft tissue and lung.
cards.a: Bone plus 400 to 1000; contrast plus 800; soft tissue plus 40 to 80; lung minus 500.

importance.why: radiology detail; helps tell contrast from calcification

cards.q: Why are window width and window level used to display CT images?
cards.a: Eye cannot see 2000 grays: a limited HU range (width) is shown around a central level, by tissue of interest.

importance.why: basis of windowing; background physics

cards.q: What window levels are used for mediastinal and lung windows?
cards.a: Mediastinal or soft tissue window: level plus 40 HU. Lung window: level minus 600 HU.

importance.why: practical CT reading; low examination yield

cards.q: Why must a chest CT be reviewed on lung windows as well as soft tissue windows?
cards.a: Lung windows show detailed lung parenchyma, which cannot be seen on soft tissue windows.
points: not seen on soft tissue windows

importance.why: parenchymal disease is missed on mediastinal windows alone

cards.q: What is IV contrast used for in CT?
cards.a: To define vascular structures.

importance.why: contrast decides whether aortic pathology can be seen

cards.q: How does a conventional CT scanner acquire its slices?
cards.a: Source and detectors cannot rotate continuously; the table moves a set distance, stopping between slices.

importance.why: historical scanner design; background

cards.q: What do slip rings allow in a spiral CT scanner?
cards.a: No physical tube-to-power-cable connection, so the ring rotates in one direction indefinitely while the table moves continuously.

importance.why: scanner engineering; background

cards.q: What are the advantages of spiral over conventional CT?
cards.a: Faster, higher-resolution images allowing coronary, pulmonary and vascular angiography; any plane and 3D reconstruction.

importance.why: explains why CT angiography and 3D reconstruction exist; background

cards.q: How does a multislice CT scanner differ from a spiral scanner?
cards.a: Several rows of detectors instead of a single row, and much faster tube rotation.

importance.why: scanner design; background

cards.q: An unstable, uncooperative patient needs vascular CT imaging: which scanner, and why?
cards.a: Multislice CT: acquisition is several times faster, minimizing scan time and movement artefact.

importance.why: choosing the scanner for the unstable patient; minor point

cards.q: What does the better resolution of multislice CT allow?
cards.a: Video footage, for example of the valves.

importance.why: technical detail; rarely asked

cards.q: Why is a chest CT important before a cardiac reoperation?
cards.a: It identifies structures at risk during sternal re-entry: patent grafts, aorta and RV.

importance.why: injury on re-entry can be fatal; CT plans the approach; a classic viva question

cards.q: A valve patient at low risk of coronary disease needs preoperative coronary assessment: what test may replace catheterization?
cards.a: CT coronary angiography.

importance.why: changes the preoperative work-up of valve patients

cards.q: How accurate is CT angiography for coronary disease?
cards.a: Very specific and sensitive.

importance.why: justifies its use to exclude coronary disease

cards.q: Why is CT coronary angiography of little use in patients at higher risk of coronary disease?
cards.a: Any significant abnormality must then be evaluated with standard coronary angiography anyway.

importance.why: selecting the right coronary test before valve surgery

cards.q: How do contrast load and radiation exposure compare between invasive and CT coronary angiography?
cards.a: Very similar.

importance.why: CT angiography does not spare contrast or radiation; minor point

cards.q: List the uses of chest CT in cardiac surgical patients.
cards.a: Reoperations; coronary assessment in low-risk valve patients; aortic aneurysm and dissection; mediastinitis, sternal dehiscence, PE.

importance.why: frames every perioperative CT request

cards.q: After sternotomy a patient is suspected of mediastinitis or sternal dehiscence: what imaging helps?
cards.a: Chest CT, which also evaluates PE.

importance.why: post-sternotomy complications are evaluated by CT

cards.q: A patient is suspected of an aortic aneurysm or dissection: what investigation diagnoses and evaluates it?
cards.a: Chest CT.

importance.why: a missed dissection kills; CT decides the operation

cards.q: What can and cannot a non-contrast chest CT show about an aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: Calcification in the aortic wall, but little other information about the vessel lumen.

importance.why: a non-contrast scan can hide a dissection

cards.q: A non-contrast CT shows a large aortic aneurysm: why repeat it with IV contrast?
cards.a: Non-contrast shows little of the lumen; contrast can reveal a dissection, e.g. type B with intraluminal thrombus.

importance.why: only contrast shows the dissection; missing it can kill

cards.q: What can a 3D CT reconstruction of an aneurysmal ascending aorta show?
cards.a: The right coronary artery in the atrioventricular groove.

importance.why: illustrative figure; useful for planning only

cards.q: How is cardiac catheterization classified?
cards.a: Right and/or left heart; diagnostic or therapeutic.

importance.why: framework for the topic; background

cards.q: What are the access routes for left and right heart catheterization?
cards.a: Left: femoral or radial artery. Right: femoral, internal jugular or subclavian vein.
points: femoral, internal jugular or subclavian vein

importance.why: access site determines access complications

cards.q: What does left heart catheterization measure?
cards.a: LA, LV and aortic pressures; transmitral and transaortic gradients; mitral and aortic valve areas.

importance.why: basis of invasive valve assessment

cards.q: What is the commonest indication for left heart catheterization?
cards.a: Coronary angiography.

importance.why: simple fact; background

cards.q: How does ventriculography differ from coronary angiography in contrast use?
cards.a: Ventriculography requires substantially more contrast.

importance.why: explains why ventriculography is avoided in renal dysfunction

cards.q: What therapeutic procedures are done by left heart catheterization?
cards.a: PCI; balloon mitral valvuloplasty; TAVI; LA appendage occlusion.

importance.why: the percutaneous alternatives to surgery

cards.q: What is right heart catheterization essentially the same as?
cards.a: Floating a Swan-Ganz catheter.

importance.why: simple equivalence; background

cards.q: What does right heart catheterization measure?
cards.a: RA, RV and PA pressures, PAWP, and saturations including mixed venous saturation (SvO2).

importance.why: basis of pulmonary hypertension and shunt assessment

cards.q: What can be calculated or done at right heart catheterization?
cards.a: PVR, cardiac output and shunts; pulmonary angiography; transseptal puncture for LA access.

importance.why: PVR and shunts change operability

cards.q: A patient has an acute type A dissection: is cardiac catheterization appropriate?
cards.a: The patient may be too unwell to tolerate it; otherwise contraindications to catheterization are few.

importance.why: delaying a type A repair for catheterization can be fatal

cards.q: A patient with aortic stenosis or mobile vegetations is having catheterization: what must be avoided, and why?
cards.a: Ventriculography and pull-back gradients: crossing the aortic valve risks stroke; echo gives hemodynamics more safely.

importance.why: crossing a stenotic or infected valve can cause a stroke

cards.q: A patient with renal dysfunction needs catheterization: what should be avoided, and why?
cards.a: Ventriculography: the increased contrast load significantly worsens renal impairment.

importance.why: contrast nephropathy before surgery worsens outcome

cards.q: Describe the setup for coronary angiography.
cards.a: Patient awake but sedated and supine; sheath access by a modified Seldinger technique.

importance.why: procedural background for a surgeon

cards.q: How is contrast delivered to the coronary arteries at angiography?
cards.a: Injected into each coronary ostium in turn via a size 4 Judkins catheter, 2 to 3 mm in diameter.

importance.why: procedural background

cards.q: How are the different angiographic views obtained?
cards.a: X-ray tube and camera sit opposite each other on a C-arm, rotated cranially, caudally and left to right.

importance.why: explains view names used to read angiograms

cards.q: What is the advantage of biplane imaging?
cards.a: Two cameras give simultaneous images from two angles, reducing radiation exposure.

importance.why: technical background

cards.q: How are angiographic moving images recorded today?
cards.a: On digital CDs, which have superseded cine film.

importance.why: historical detail; trivial

cards.q: What antiplatelet doses may be given around PCI?
cards.a: Clopidogrel 300 mg or aspirin 75 mg, before and after PCI.

importance.why: antiplatelet load after PCI matters for surgical bleeding

cards.q: Which catheterization complications need emergency bypass surgery, and how often?
cards.a: LAD dissection, acute LAD occlusion and cardiac tamponade; 1 in 1000 catheterizations.

importance.why: a crash call to theatre that kills if delayed; classic viva

cards.q: What are the rates of major adverse events and death after cardiac catheterization?
cards.a: Major adverse events such as stroke 1%; death 0.01%.

importance.why: risk figures for consent and decision

cards.q: What happens if the puncture site is not occluded after catheter removal?
cards.a: Extensive hematoma, which may be retroperitoneal if the femoral puncture was high.

importance.why: a missed retroperitoneal bleed can be fatal

cards.q: What general rules apply when reviewing a coronary angiogram?
cards.a: Look at each lesion in several views and at the whole film; comment on the vessels systematically.

importance.why: a systematic reading prevents missed lesions

cards.q: Why must an eccentric plaque be viewed in several projections?
cards.a: It looks most significant end on and may almost disappear when viewed perpendicularly.

importance.why: a single view can hide a significant lesion

cards.q: Why may angiography underestimate stenosis in diffusely diseased vessels?
cards.a: Lesions are judged against adjacent 'normal' segments, which in diffuse disease are themselves diseased.

importance.why: underestimation leads to an inadequate revascularization plan

cards.q: What area reductions correspond to 50%, 70% and 90% diameter stenoses?
cards.a: 75%, 90% and 99% respectively.

importance.why: classic numbers behind stenosis grading

cards.q: When is a coronary stenosis significant, and why?
cards.a: When more than 50% of lumen diameter, because it reduces the normal 3 to 4 times flow reserve.

importance.why: the threshold that defines operable coronary disease

cards.q: What is the effect of a more than 70% diameter stenosis on coronary flow?
cards.a: It eliminates any capacity to increase flow above resting flow.

importance.why: the tight-stenosis threshold that drives grafting

cards.q: What TIMI flow does a more than 90% stenosis usually produce?
cards.a: TIMI grade 1 or 2 flow.

importance.why: links stenosis severity to the TIMI scale

cards.q: An apparently occluded vessel appears late on injection of another vessel: what is happening?
cards.a: Retrograde filling: most commonly PDA and RCA from the LAD, sometimes LAD from the PDA.

importance.why: shows the occluded vessel's distal bed, a possible graft target

cards.q: The LAD looks completely occluded on one view: what pitfall must you exclude, and how?
cards.a: A large diagonal mistaken for an occluded LAD: always look at the LAO view before commenting on the LAD.

importance.why: misreading the LAD changes the operation

cards.q: How do you open your presentation of a coronary angiogram?
cards.a: With a summary after viewing all views, e.g. a 75-year-old man with 3-vessel disease and moderate LV.

importance.why: structure of a viva angiogram presentation

cards.q: In which views are the left main stem and the circumflex best seen?
cards.a: LMS: RAO and LAO caudal. Circumflex: RAO.

importance.why: knowing the best view avoids missing left main disease

cards.q: In which view are the LAD and diagonals best seen?
cards.a: The LAO cranial view.

importance.why: best view for the LAD, the most important graft target

cards.q: After the summary, in what order do you describe a coronary angiogram?
cards.a: LMS; circumflex system; LAD and diagonals; RCA and PDA with dominance; then ventricular function.

importance.why: systematic report used in every viva angiogram

cards.q: Apart from the coronary lesions, what else do you describe on an angiogram?
cards.a: Ventricular function, any regional akinesia, MR, and calcification of the coronaries or valves.

importance.why: LV function and MR change the operation

cards.q: Which projections are used to image the coronary arteries?
cards.a: PA, RAO and LAO views, angled cranially or caudally.

importance.why: naming of views; background

cards.q: What systematic approach avoids common mistakes when reading coronary angiograms?
cards.a: Identify each view; look at all views; each vessel in multiple views; the whole clip, as some vessels fill late.

importance.why: systematic reading prevents misinterpretation

cards.q: How do you tell a RAO from a LAO view?
cards.a: RAO: ribs go down to the right, image right of spine. LAO: ribs down to the left, image left of spine.
points: RAO ribs down to the right
LAO ribs down to the left

importance.why: view recognition in the angiogram viva

cards.q: How do you tell a cranial from a caudal angiographic view?
cards.a: Cranial: the diaphragm is superimposed over most of the picture. Caudal: it is hardly seen.

importance.why: view recognition in the angiogram viva

cards.q: How do you identify the circumflex on any angiographic view?
cards.a: It is the vessel closest to the spine, or to the catheter in the descending aorta: the most posterior vessel.

importance.why: vessel identification for grafting decisions

cards.q: How do you identify the LAD on an angiogram?
cards.a: It travels towards the apex, is usually the longest vessel, and gives septals at 90 degrees.

importance.why: identifying the LAD, the key graft target

cards.q: On a RAO view of the right coronary, how do you distinguish the PDA from the LVB?
cards.a: The PDA gives off short septals at 90 degrees.

importance.why: fine angiographic detail

cards.q: Name the branches of the right coronary artery in order.
cards.a: Conus; SA nodal; RV branch; acute marginal; AV nodal; PDA; LVB or posterolateral branches.

importance.why: coronary anatomy is the foundation of every CABG; classic

cards.q: How often does the AV nodal artery arise from the RCA, and how often from the circumflex?
cards.a: RCA 60%; circumflex 40%.

importance.why: anatomical variant relevant to conduction injury

cards.q: Which artery gives the PDA in right- and left-dominant patients, and how common is each?
cards.a: Right-dominant (85%): the RCA. Left-dominant (10%): the circumflex.

importance.why: dominance is described on every angiogram; classic viva

cards.q: What branches does the posterior descending artery give, and at what angle?
cards.a: Inferior septals, coming off at 90 degrees.

importance.why: helps identify the PDA on angiography

cards.q: How is the RCA divided into proximal, mid and distal segments?
cards.a: Proximal up to the RV branch; mid up to the acute marginal; distal up to the bifurcation.

importance.why: segment naming used in reports and graft planning

cards.q: How does the left main stem divide?
cards.a: Into LAD and circumflex; occasionally it trifurcates, with a ramus intermediate branch.

importance.why: basic left coronary anatomy

cards.q: What branches arise from the LAD and from the circumflex?
cards.a: LAD: septals at 90 degrees and diagonals. Circumflex: obtuse marginals, AV nodal (40%), and in left dominance PDA and LVB.

importance.why: graft targets on the left system; foundation anatomy

cards.q: How is the LAD divided into proximal, mid and distal segments?
cards.a: Proximal up to the 1st septal; mid until the 2nd diagonal; distal after the 2nd diagonal.

importance.why: proximal LAD disease changes the indication for surgery

cards.q: What are the five common angiographic views?
cards.a: RAO and LAO of the right coronary; RAO, LAO and LAO caudal ('spider view') of the left coronary system.

importance.why: view names used in the angiogram viva

cards.q: Stenosis severity looks uncertain on angiography: what further assessment helps?
cards.a: Pressure measurements such as fractional flow reserve (FFR), and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS).

importance.why: physiology refines the indication for revascularization

cards.q: Echocardiography is equivocal: what can cardiac catheterization add?
cards.a: Severity of valve lesions, pulmonary hypertension, ventricular function and intracardiac shunts.

importance.why: resolves doubt before deciding on surgery

cards.q: What is fractional flow reserve?
cards.a: Essentially the ratio between blood pressure proximal and distal to a lesion, measured at maximal flow.

importance.why: standard physiological test of a stenosis

cards.q: A borderline stenosis is assessed with FFR: what value means the lesion is significant?
cards.a: Less than 75%, i.e. less than 75% of maximal flow in a non-diseased coronary.

importance.why: a key threshold that decides intervention

cards.q: What does evidence suggest for lesions with an FFR above the significance threshold?
cards.a: Some data suggest it is safe to watch rather than intervene.

importance.why: avoids unnecessary intervention; evidence base

cards.q: How is maximal flow induced for FFR, and what does the test therefore assess?
cards.a: Adenosine or papaverine, normally 4 to 5 times resting flow; so it assesses coronary reserve.

importance.why: mechanism of the FFR test

cards.q: Classify coronary flow by the TIMI scale.
cards.a: 0 no antegrade flow; 1 penetration, incomplete distal filling; 2 delayed but complete filling; 3 normal flow.

importance.why: a classic named classification

cards.q: Angiography shows delayed but complete distal filling: what TIMI grade?
cards.a: TIMI 2, partial reperfusion.

importance.why: applying the TIMI scale

cards.q: Contrast penetrates a lesion but fills the distal bed incompletely: what TIMI grade?
cards.a: TIMI 1, penetration without perfusion.

importance.why: applying the TIMI scale

cards.q: How would you measure the transaortic valve gradient at catheterization?
cards.a: LV pressure with simultaneous aortic pressure distal to the valve, or by pulling the catheter back into the aorta.

importance.why: invasive aortic stenosis assessment

cards.q: Which aortic valve gradient is the most physiologic?
cards.a: The mean gradient.

importance.why: the gradient to quote when grading stenosis

cards.q: How would you measure the mitral valve gradient at catheterization?
cards.a: Simultaneous PAWP or LA pressure (by transseptal puncture) and LV end-diastolic pressure.

importance.why: invasive mitral stenosis assessment

cards.q: How is valve area calculated at catheterization?
cards.a: Gorlin equation: area equals flow over velocity, or cardiac output over the square root of the gradient.

importance.why: named equation; classic viva

cards.q: Valve area must be estimated in a low cardiac output state: what is the problem, and what helps?
cards.a: Cardiac output estimation is particularly open to error; dobutamine stress testing is a diagnostic adjunct.

importance.why: low-flow stenosis can be misgraded and the operation wrongly declined

cards.q: Describe the Grossman grading of regurgitation.
cards.a: I faint, clears in one beat; II proximal less than distal; III equal; IV dense, proximal greater than distal.
points: I faint, clears in one beat

importance.why: named angiographic grading of regurgitation

cards.q: Opacification of the proximal chamber equals the distal chamber: what Grossman grade of regurgitation?
cards.a: Grade III.

importance.why: applying the Grossman scale

cards.q: What methods can measure cardiac output during catheterization?
cards.a: Thermodilution, the Fick principle and angiographic methods; all have potential errors.

importance.why: cardiac output underlies valve area and PVR

cards.q: Describe the thermodilution technique of measuring cardiac output.
cards.a: Saline bolus into proximal port, measured at a distal port; equation uses specific gravity and temperatures of fluid and blood.

importance.why: technique used daily on ICU

cards.q: What are the sources of error in thermodilution cardiac output?
cards.a: Tricuspid regurgitation, incorrect injection technique, and low cardiac output.

importance.why: misleading output leads to wrong treatment

cards.q: State the Fick principle.
cards.a: Uptake or release of a substance, usually VO2, equals the arteriovenous concentration gradient times cardiac output.

importance.why: classic physiology principle

cards.q: What oxygen consumption is assumed in most labs for the Fick method?
cards.a: 125 mL/m2; VO2 is usually not measured.

importance.why: a lab assumption; detail

cards.q: In a low output state, which method of measuring cardiac output is more accurate?
cards.a: The Fick method, more accurate than thermodilution.

importance.why: choosing the right output method

cards.q: A patient with MR or AI, or on supplemental oxygen, needs cardiac output measured: can you use Fick?
cards.a: No: the Fick method should not be used in MR, AI, or patients receiving supplemental oxygen.

importance.why: a wrong method gives a wrong cardiac output

cards.q: How is cardiac output measured angiographically?
cards.a: Trace the LV end-diastolic and end-systolic images and convert them to volume by modelling.

importance.why: technical detail

cards.q: How is pulmonary vascular resistance calculated, and what is normal?
cards.a: (Mean PAP minus mean LAP) over cardiac output; PAWP replaces LAP without pulmonary disease; normal 3 Wood units.

importance.why: PVR decides operability, e.g. in valve disease and transplant

cards.q: Pulmonary hypertension is found at catheterization: how do you decide whether it is fixed?
cards.a: Fixed pulmonary hypertension cannot be reversed with NTG, inhaled NO, Flolan or exercise.

importance.why: fixed pulmonary hypertension can make surgery prohibitive

cards.q: Which two conditions can cardiac catheterization help differentiate?
cards.a: Restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis.

importance.why: decides whether pericardial surgery can help

cards.q: How are intracardiac shunts detected and quantified at catheterization?
cards.a: Oximetry sampling from IVC, SVC, multiple RA sites, PA, coronary sinus and artery.

importance.why: shunt size decides repair

cards.q: How is Qp:Qs calculated?
cards.a: (SaO2 minus MVO2) divided by (PVO2 minus PAO2).

importance.why: classic shunt formula

cards.q: On simultaneous LV and aortic traces, how do the peak instantaneous, peak-to-peak and mean gradients compare?
cards.a: They differ: in the book's example peak instantaneous 100, peak-to-peak 50 and mean 60 mmHg.

importance.why: different gradients give different numbers for the same valve

cards.q: On a catheter pressure trace, which traces define the mean transmitral gradient?
cards.a: The LA and LV pressure traces.

importance.why: figure detail of invasive mitral assessment

cards.q: What is echocardiography, and what are its two main approaches?
cards.a: Ultrasound used to assess cardiac conditions; transthoracic (TTE) and transesophageal (TEE).

importance.why: every cardiac surgical patient is assessed by echo; basic definition

cards.q: Name the echo modalities in common use.
cards.a: B-mode (2D), M-mode, D-mode (Doppler), colour flow imaging and 3D echo.

importance.why: basic terminology, background for reading reports

cards.q: What is B-mode echo?
cards.a: Brightness mode, also called 2D or real-time: a 2D grayscale picture of a single plane; echo intensity shown as brightness.

importance.why: terminology only; low decision value

cards.q: Compare M-mode with B-mode echo.
cards.a: M-mode is more accurate, so used for measurements, but gives only a 1D image of structures against time.

importance.why: background physics behind the normal M-mode ranges

cards.q: What does Doppler echo measure, and what does it let you calculate?
cards.a: Flow velocities from Doppler frequency shifts, hence gradients and valve areas; only moving targets are displayed.

importance.why: the basis of every valve gradient and area used to grade stenosis

cards.q: What is duplex ultrasound?
cards.a: Doppler combined with grayscale images, to correlate flow with fixed structures.

importance.why: terminology only

cards.q: What is colour flow imaging, and what colour convention is used?
cards.a: Colour-enhanced duplex Doppler combining M-mode and D-mode with flow imaging; flow away blue, towards red (BART).

importance.why: needed to read regurgitant jets on every echo; BART is a common quick question

cards.q: When is 3D echo particularly useful?
cards.a: Viewing the morphology of the mitral valve.

importance.why: helps plan mitral valve surgery

cards.q: What ultrasound frequency range is used in echocardiography?
cards.a: 2–5 MHz; it passes through tissues and is reflected from tissue interfaces.

importance.why: physics background, rarely changes management

cards.q: How do piezoelectric crystals produce an echo image?
cards.a: As transducers they generate and detect ultrasound, converting electrical to mechanical energy and back; reflections form the image.

importance.why: basic physics, background only

cards.q: Explain the Doppler effect as used in echocardiography.
cards.a: Frequency rises as the target approaches, falls as it recedes; shift is proportional to speed, shown as sound or colour.

importance.why: principle behind every Doppler gradient; physics question at the start of an echo topic

cards.q: Why are particular echo views needed to assess some structures?
cards.a: The ultrasound frequencies used cannot penetrate air or bone.

importance.why: explains poor windows and the need for TEE

cards.q: State the Bernoulli equation for a transvalvular gradient.
cards.a: Gradient in mmHg equals 4 times vm squared, vm being the mean blood velocity in m/s.

importance.why: classic viva equation; the gradient grades stenosis and so the decision to replace the valve

cards.q: How is valve area calculated by the continuity equation?
cards.a: Valve area (cm²) equals stroke volume divided by (ejection time times 85 times mean velocity).

importance.why: valve area grades stenosis; formula is asked but rarely calculated by the surgeon

cards.q: In aortic stenosis, how is the mean transvalvular gradient estimated from peak velocity?
cards.a: Mean gradient equals 2.4 times maximum velocity squared.

importance.why: links echo velocity to AS severity

cards.q: What can be calculated from septal and posterior wall thickness in systole and diastole?
cards.a: Fractional shortening and LV mass; echo measures cardiac dimensions precisely.

importance.why: measurement background

cards.q: What is fractional shortening, and how does it differ from ejection fraction?
cards.a: A crude index of LV systolic function, expressed as a percentage but not to be confused with ejection fraction.
points: crude index of LV systolic function

importance.why: common confusion when reading LV function on reports

cards.q: What are the normal adult LV end-systolic and end-diastolic diameters on M-mode?
cards.a: End-systolic 25–41 mm; end-diastolic 35–56 mm.

importance.why: LV dilatation beyond normal informs the timing of valve surgery

cards.q: Give the normal shortening fraction and ejection fraction on M-mode.
cards.a: Shortening fraction 30–40%; ejection fraction 50–65%.

importance.why: LV function is quoted for every patient and enters risk scores

cards.q: What is the normal LV mass on echo?

importance.why: a table number rarely used in surgical decisions

cards.q: What are the normal aortic root diameter and aortic cusp separation on echo?
cards.a: Aortic root 20–37 mm; cusp separation 15–26 mm.

importance.why: tells a dilated root or restricted cusps from normal

cards.q: What are the normal left atrial and right ventricular dimensions on M-mode?
cards.a: Left atrium 19–40 mm; right ventricle 7–23 mm.

importance.why: reference numbers, low decision value

cards.q: How is LV function assessed on echo, qualitatively and quantitatively?
cards.a: Qualitative: wall motion scoring, graded normal, mild, moderate or severe impairment; quantitative: fractional shortening, ejection fraction.

importance.why: LV grade is reported for every patient and drives risk and operative planning

cards.q: What is the limitation of quantitative echo measures of LV function?
cards.a: Fractional shortening and ejection fraction are still subject to operator variability.

importance.why: explains discordant LV function between studies

cards.q: What model is used for regional wall motion assessment on echo?
cards.a: A nine-segment model.

importance.why: descriptive detail

cards.q: What is stress echocardiography, and what information does it give?
cards.a: Stressing the myocardium chemically or by exercise to assess myocardial viability and regional perfusion.

importance.why: one of the main viability tests before revascularization

cards.q: What are the drawbacks of treadmill exercise protocols for stress echo?
cards.a: Treadmill protocols such as Bruce give limited time to image the heart, and hyperventilation may make imaging difficult.

importance.why: technical detail of the test

cards.q: What is the main drug in pharmacological stress echocardiography?
cards.a: Dobutamine, in incremental low- or high-dose protocols.

importance.why: dobutamine stress is the usual viability test

cards.q: On stress echo a segment shows net outward systolic motion and does not thicken. What does it mean?
cards.a: The segment is infarcted.

importance.why: infarcted segments gain nothing from a graft

cards.q: A segment contracts normally at rest but its motion falls during stress. What does this suggest?
cards.a: Flow-limiting coronary stenosis.

importance.why: inducible ischemia is the indication for revascularization; classic stress test interpretation

cards.q: A segment impaired at rest improves on low-dose dobutamine. What does it contain?
cards.a: Stunned or hibernating myocardium.

importance.why: contractile reserve marks viable muscle worth revascularizing; a classic viability question

cards.q: Critical aortic stenosis with only a moderate gradient: the gradient rises on stress echo. What does that tell you?
cards.a: The myocardium will respond well to aortic valve replacement.

importance.why: decides whether a low-gradient AS patient should have valve replacement

cards.q: How can ischemia on stress echo cause mitral regurgitation?
cards.a: Papillary muscle ischemia from an inducible septal or posterior wall motion defect.
points: septal or posterior wall motion defect

importance.why: explains ischemic MR seen on stress testing

cards.q: What resolution does TEE achieve compared with TTE?
cards.a: Finer than TTE, down to 2–3 mm.

importance.why: explains why TEE is preferred for detail

cards.q: You must exclude left atrial appendage thrombus or assess the ascending aorta. TTE or TEE, and why?
cards.a: TEE: it images the posterior heart, such as LA appendage thrombus, and the ascending aorta better than TTE.

importance.why: missed LA appendage thrombus means embolic stroke; choosing the right test changes the work-up

cards.q: How is TEE performed, and what are its relative contraindications?
cards.a: Under light sedation; esophageal strictures, pouches and varices, respiratory compromise, cervical pathology.

importance.why: TEE in the wrong patient can perforate the esophagus or compromise the airway

cards.q: A patient with an esophageal stricture needs a TEE. How would you proceed?
cards.a: A stricture is a relative contraindication; if TEE is done, use a pediatric probe.

importance.why: changes how the test is done safely

cards.q: How can you tell a TEE image from a TTE image?
cards.a: Labelled films; in TEE the left atrium sits at the image apex, nearest the transducer; AV valves concave downwards.

importance.why: image-reading orientation, a viva picture opener

cards.q: On a TEE image, what does the apex of the triangle represent, and which chamber lies there?
cards.a: The probe in the esophagus, i.e. posterior; the left atrium is almost always at the apex.

importance.why: orientation on any TEE picture shown in the viva

cards.q: On TEE, which structures are most anterior, and what lies next to the aortic valve?
cards.a: The right ventricle and atrium are most anterior; the aortic valve is adjacent to the anterior mitral leaflet.

importance.why: relation of aortic valve to anterior mitral leaflet matters in valve surgery

cards.q: In the TEE short-axis view, where does the inter-atrial septum point?
cards.a: At the non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve.

importance.why: identifies the aortic cusps on TEE

cards.q: In the TEE long-axis view, how do you locate the aortic valve?
cards.a: It may lie left or right depending on probe orientation, but is always adjacent to the interventricular septum.
points: left or right with probe orientation

importance.why: orientation tip for TEE images

cards.q: What affects TTE image quality?
cards.a: Patient build (obese, emphysematous, postoperative), patient position, probe position and contact, machine settings.

importance.why: explains poor TTE windows and when to move to TEE

cards.q: What happens if the Doppler beam is not aligned parallel to blood flow?
cards.a: Velocity is underestimated, and hence the transvalvular gradient.

importance.why: underestimated gradient under-grades stenosis and can delay surgery

cards.q: What error results from aligning the beam obliquely across a chamber?
cards.a: The chamber size is overestimated.

importance.why: measurement error, informs interpretation

cards.q: What error can eccentric jets or poor views cause in Doppler measurement?
cards.a: Measuring the wrong signal instead of the main flow, e.g. an MR jet mistaken for AS.

importance.why: a misread jet can lead to the wrong valve operation

cards.q: How is valvular regurgitation graded on echo?
cards.a: By a number of qualitative and quantitative variables, such as jet size and regurgitant fraction.

importance.why: opener to the regurgitation grading questions

cards.q: What are the echo criteria for severe aortic regurgitation?
cards.a: Central jet width more than 65% of LVOT; regurgitant fraction more than 50%.
points: jet width more than 65% of LVOT

importance.why: severe AR is the threshold for considering valve surgery; key numbers

cards.q: What are the echo criteria for mild aortic regurgitation, and how is moderate defined?
cards.a: Mild: jet width less than 25% of LVOT, regurgitant fraction less than 30%; moderate: values in between.
points: jet width less than 25% of LVOT

importance.why: completes the AR grading

cards.q: Give the quantitative echo thresholds for severe mitral regurgitation.
cards.a: Central jet more than 40% of LA area, regurgitant fraction more than 50%, ERO more than 40 mm².
points: jet more than 40% of LA area

importance.why: severe MR is the threshold for mitral surgery; key numbers

cards.q: Besides jet size, which two echo signs indicate severe mitral regurgitation?
cards.a: Jet impinging on the LA wall; systolic flow reversal in the pulmonary veins.
points: systolic flow reversal in pulmonary veins

importance.why: qualitative signs of severe MR that support operating

cards.q: What are the echo criteria for mild mitral regurgitation, and how is moderate defined?
cards.a: Mild: central jet less than 20% of LA area, regurgitant fraction less than 30%; moderate: values in between.
points: jet less than 20% of LA area

importance.why: completes the MR grading

cards.q: How many standard TOE views are there?
cards.a: 20 standard views.

importance.why: TOE nomenclature background

cards.q: Name six mid-oesophageal TOE views.
cards.a: Four chamber, two chamber, long axis, mitral commissural, aortic valve short axis, bicaval.

importance.why: intraoperative TOE views the surgeon reads in theatre

cards.q: Besides mid-oesophageal views, name three other standard TOE views.
cards.a: Transgastric basal short axis, transgastric long axis, and the aortic valve long-axis view.

importance.why: TOE nomenclature

cards.q: In TOE nomenclature, what do ME, TG, LAX and SAX stand for?
cards.a: Mid-oesophageal, transgastric, long axis, short axis.

importance.why: abbreviations used in every TOE report

cards.q: What structures does the mid-oesophageal four-chamber view show?
cards.a: Both atria, both ventricles, the tricuspid valve and the mitral leaflets.

importance.why: standard view, image-reading detail

cards.q: What structures does the mid-oesophageal long-axis view show?
cards.a: LA, LV, LVOT, ascending aorta, RV and the mitral leaflets A2 and P2.

importance.why: standard view, image-reading detail

cards.q: Which mitral segments does the mid-oesophageal mitral commissural view show?
cards.a: P3, A2 and P1, with the LA, LV and coronary sinus.

importance.why: segment identification guides mitral repair

cards.q: What does the mid-oesophageal aortic valve short-axis view show?
cards.a: The non-coronary, left and right coronary cusps, with the LA, RA and tricuspid valve.

importance.why: aortic valve anatomy on TOE

cards.q: What does the mid-oesophageal bicaval view show?
cards.a: Left atrium, right atrium, superior and inferior vena cava.

importance.why: standard view, image-reading detail

cards.q: In TOE labelling, what do A1, A2, P1 and P3 denote?
cards.a: Segments of the anterior (A) and posterior (P) mitral leaflets.

importance.why: mitral segment naming used in repair planning

cards.q: What 1970s observation challenged the view that chronic ventricular dysfunction meant infarction?
cards.a: That chronic ventricular dysfunction could be reversed by revascularization.

importance.why: historical evidence behind viability testing

cards.q: What did the term 'hibernating myocardium' originally describe?
cards.a: The theory that chronic LV dysfunction was an adaptive response to chronically reduced coronary flow at rest.
points: chronically reduced coronary flow at rest

importance.why: definition underlying viability assessment

cards.q: What do more recent studies suggest is the mechanism of hibernation?
cards.a: Repetitive stunning: adequate perfusion at rest, ischemia on exercise from impaired coronary flow reserve.

importance.why: mechanism question that follows the definition

cards.q: What are the characteristics of hibernating myocardium?
cards.a: Reduced contractility (hypokinesis, not akinesis); reduced perfusion, mainly on exercise; viable; improves with revascularization.

importance.why: recognising hibernation decides whether revascularization will help; classic list

cards.q: In hibernating myocardium, what wall motion shows that the muscle is viable?
cards.a: Hypokinesis rather than akinesis: the muscle is viable, not infarcted.

importance.why: separates viable from infarcted segments

cards.q: What is contractile reserve, and what does it predict?
cards.a: Improvement with inotropes or exercise; it can predict functional improvement after revascularization.

importance.why: contractile reserve is the viability signal on stress testing

cards.q: Poor LV function, mainly breathless rather than anginal, considered for CABG. What must you assess?
cards.a: Myocardial viability (hibernating myocardium): detecting it is clinically important in this group before CABG.

importance.why: viability decides whether high-risk CABG is worth doing; classic viva case

cards.q: In poor LV function, what does absence of viability imply for high-risk CABG?
cards.a: Much lower prognostic and symptomatic benefit from the surgery.

importance.why: operating on non-viable myocardium exposes the patient to high risk for little gain

cards.q: What are the key modalities for assessing myocardial viability?
cards.a: Nuclear imaging, stress echocardiography and MRI.

importance.why: a standard list asked before the details of each test

cards.q: What does nuclear cardiac imaging allow, and what isotopes are used?
cards.a: Ventriculography and perfusion studies; gamma-ray or positron-emitting radionuclides.

importance.why: background to nuclear tests

cards.q: Which technetium compounds are replacing thallium in nuclear perfusion imaging?
cards.a: Technetium-99m compounds such as sestamibi and tetrofosmin, replacing cheaper thallium-201 compounds.

importance.why: tracer detail, rarely decisive

cards.q: How does conventional radionuclide imaging produce perfusion images?
cards.a: Tracer taken up by red cells decays to gamma rays, hitting a sodium iodide crystal; a photomultiplier detects scintillations.

importance.why: physics background

cards.q: What is SPECT?
cards.a: Two gamma cameras with computerized reconstruction, so technetium or thallium images can be reconstructed in any plane.

importance.why: technique background

cards.q: How is a SPECT perfusion study sequenced?
cards.a: Stress imaging first (exercise, dobutamine, dipyridamole or adenosine); if normal, rest imaging is not needed.

importance.why: test protocol detail

cards.q: Stress SPECT is abnormal and rest images are taken. How do you read fixed and reversible defects?
cards.a: Fixed defects represent infarcts; reversible defects suggest hibernation.

importance.why: the core interpretation that decides whether revascularization will help

cards.q: What tracer is most widely used in cardiac PET, and what does it reflect?
cards.a: 18F-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose, taken up by myocytes, reflecting glucose metabolism during ischemia.

importance.why: PET-FDG is a recognised viability test

cards.q: Compare PET with SPECT for myocardial imaging.
cards.a: PET has much better spatial resolution than SPECT's 1 cm, but routine use is limited by very high cost.

importance.why: comparison question, low decision value

cards.q: Which technetium-99m compounds are used in cardiac nuclear imaging, and for what?
cards.a: Labeled red cells, MIBI and pyrophosphate: blood pool studies, ventriculography and myocardial perfusion.

importance.why: table detail, rarely asked

cards.q: Which radionuclides are used to image hibernation?
cards.a: Thallium-201 (thallium chloride) and 18F-FDG.

importance.why: the viability tracers

cards.q: What are nitrogen-13 and the oxygen radionuclide used to image?
cards.a: Nitrogen-13: myocardial perfusion; the oxygen radionuclide: oxygen uptake.

importance.why: rare research tracers

cards.q: What does nuclear ventriculography provide?
cards.a: An accurate, relatively non-invasive, reproducible ejection fraction, and intracardiac shunts.

importance.why: alternative EF measurement

cards.q: How is myocardial perfusion imaging performed, and with what stressors?
cards.a: Regional flow is imaged after stress then at rest; stressors adenosine, dobutamine and exercise.

importance.why: test protocol background

cards.q: Why does a flow-limiting stenosis cause a defect on stress perfusion imaging?
cards.a: During stress its territory receives relatively less blood than adjoining normal territories.

importance.why: the mechanism behind every stress perfusion result

cards.q: A perfusion defect after stress normalizes at rest. What is it, and what may help?
cards.a: A reversible defect: reversible ischemia, which may be improved by revascularization.

importance.why: a reversible defect is an indication for revascularization; classic interpretation

cards.q: A photon-deficient area is unchanged after stress and at rest. What is it, and will revascularization help?
cards.a: A fixed defect, usually infarction, which will not be improved by revascularization.

importance.why: grafting infarcted territory gives no benefit; classic interpretation

cards.q: How does cardiac MRI assess myocardial viability?
cards.a: End-diastolic wall thickness, dobutamine stress for contractile reserve, and contrast enhancement revealing scar.

importance.why: CMR is a main viability modality

cards.q: Besides viability, what does cardiac MRI measure accurately, and what can CT also show?
cards.a: LV and RV volumes and ejection fraction; CT can also show late enhancement, wall thickness and volumes.

importance.why: supporting detail on imaging

cards.q: A thallium scan shows apical defects after stress that reverse on rest images. Interpret it.
cards.a: Reversible ischemia in the apical territory.

importance.why: picture interpretation of the book's example scan

cards.q: What must be available before emergency cardiac surgery?
cards.a: ICU bed; surgeon; anesthesiology team; operating room; two scrub nurses; perfusionist; blood.

importance.why: missing a resource in an emergency delays a life-saving operation

cards.q: What should you always do with the patients on your elective list?
cards.a: Always see the patients you operate on: take your own history and do your own examination.

importance.why: basic safe practice, every patient

cards.q: What do you check before an elective cardiac list?
cards.a: Consent; bloods reviewed and cross-matched; CXR reviewed and films available; any additional investigations needed.

importance.why: every patient, avoids cancellations and unsafe surgery

cards.q: When should a preoperative echo or angiogram be repeated?
cards.a: If it is more than 6 months old.

importance.why: out-of-date imaging can miss progression and lead to the wrong operation

cards.q: How is the running order of an elective cardiac list decided?
cards.a: With the surgeon: sick, complex patients first; infection risks last; equipment availability may dictate order.

importance.why: list organisation, background

cards.q: Why are sick, complex patients placed first on the list?
cards.a: They will not tolerate cancellation and benefit from early ICU admission while imaging and support services are fully available.

importance.why: cancelling or delaying a sick patient can be dangerous

cards.q: A patient on your list is an infection risk. Where do you place them?
cards.a: Last on the list.

importance.why: limits cross-infection of later patients

cards.q: Who must know the list order, and how?
cards.a: The anesthesiologist, especially about last-minute changes; nursing staff, with a copy at every patient location, ICU and OR.
points: copy at each location, ICU and OR

importance.why: communication detail

cards.q: Besides the operation, what must you specify when writing the list?
cards.a: Radial artery and side; off-pump; redo; femoral bypass; thoracotomy and side.

importance.why: list-writing detail

cards.q: What arrangements may need to be made in advance for an elective list?
cards.a: Order homografts; contact pacing technicians for pacemaker patients; notify theatres of latex allergy.

importance.why: an unprepared latex-allergic patient risks anaphylaxis

cards.q: A patient is an outlier on a ward not used to surgery. What must the nurses know?
cards.a: Starved from midnight, in a gown, on a stretcher, and shaved at least 30 minutes before send time.

importance.why: ward logistics

cards.q: What should ICU be told about your list?
cards.a: Which patients are appropriate for fast-tracking.

importance.why: bed planning detail

cards.q: Which patient factors should you tell the perfusionist about?
cards.a: Anemia, weight less than 60 kg, and high creatinine.

importance.why: each changes how bypass is run

cards.q: A patient on your list is anemic. What do you tell the perfusionist, and what follows?
cards.a: They may prime the pump with blood, so you will need to cross-match extra.

importance.why: changes blood ordering and pump prime

cards.q: A patient weighs under 60 kg. Why tell the perfusionist?
cards.a: They may minimize the prime volume to avoid hemodilution.

importance.why: changes bypass technique

cards.q: A patient has a high creatinine. Why tell the perfusionist?
cards.a: The perfusionist can filter the patient on bypass.

importance.why: changes bypass technique

cards.q: What do risk stratification tools estimate, and which are the main ones?
cards.a: Operative risk; the main systems are EuroSCORE, the STS score and the Parsonnet score.

importance.why: risk scores are quoted at every consent and decision; a classic viva opener

cards.q: What do cardiac surgical registries publish?
cards.a: Institution- and surgeon-specific risk-adjusted mortality and complication rates, allowing for comorbidity, demographics and nature of surgery.

importance.why: governance background

cards.q: How are surgical outcome data usually published, and which outliers are highlighted?
cards.a: Raw index-operation mortality, e.g. isolated CABG, per institution or surgeon; those beyond 2 standard deviations of the risk-adjusted mean.

importance.why: outcome-reporting question in governance vivas

cards.q: What effect may publishing outcome data have had?
cards.a: Lower mortality rates, possibly through risk-averse behaviour causing bias against high-risk patients.

importance.why: controversy question, no direct effect on an operation

cards.q: Describe EuroSCORE.
cards.a: Based on European CABG patients; simple additive and more accurate logistic versions; tends to overestimate operative risk.

importance.why: the named risk score used for consent and decisions on every patient; classic viva

cards.q: What is the STS score, and how does it compare with EuroSCORE?
cards.a: A similar model validated in North American patients, freely available as an online calculator.

importance.why: second named risk score

cards.q: What is the Parsonnet score?
