cards.a: One of the earliest risk stratification systems, not widely used now.

importance.why: historical score

cards.q: When do you stop warfarin before cardiac surgery?
cards.a: 3–5 days preoperatively.

importance.why: operating on warfarin risks major bleeding; every anticoagulated patient

cards.q: A patient with a mechanical valve on warfarin needs cardiac surgery. How do you manage anticoagulation?
cards.a: Stop warfarin 3–5 days before; admit early and start heparin, stopped 6 hours before surgery.

importance.why: unbridged mechanical valve risks valve thrombosis and stroke; heparin too late risks bleeding

cards.q: When are aspirin and clopidogrel stopped before surgery in low-risk patients?
cards.a: Aspirin 5 days and clopidogrel 10 days preoperatively.

importance.why: antiplatelet bleeding is a common, avoidable cause of re-exploration

cards.q: When are ACE inhibitors withheld before cardiac surgery?
cards.a: On the day before surgery.

importance.why: routine drug instruction

cards.q: How do you manage a non-insulin-dependent diabetic before cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Normal medication, but withhold long-acting hypoglycaemics such as gliclazide on the morning of surgery.

importance.why: avoids perioperative hypoglycaemia in a common patient group

cards.q: How do you manage an insulin-dependent diabetic on your list?
cards.a: First on the list; morning insulin replaced by a sliding scale and iv fluids.

importance.why: changes list order and insulin regimen; hypo- or hyperglycaemia harms

cards.q: Which patients need a carotid Doppler before cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Those with a history of CVA, TIA or severe peripheral vascular disease.

importance.why: screening for carotid disease prevents perioperative stroke; classic pre-op question

cards.q: When may carotid intervention be indicated before cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Internal carotid stenosis more than 70%, especially if the other side is tightly stenosed, to reduce CVA risk.

importance.why: threshold that decides carotid intervention to prevent stroke

cards.q: A CABG patient has significant carotid disease. Whom do you involve, and what do you do on bypass?
cards.a: Discuss with a vascular surgeon; maintain high perfusion pressures.

importance.why: high perfusion pressure protects the brain on bypass

cards.q: A patient on your list has a murmur. What do you check?
cards.a: A recent preoperative TTE, which all patients should have: review it.

importance.why: unrecognised valve disease leads to the wrong operation

cards.q: A patient has unexplained anemia before elective cardiac surgery. What do you do?
cards.a: Full outpatient investigation; the surgeon may prime the pump with blood; not normally transfused preoperatively.

importance.why: unexplained anemia may be a hidden pathology; changes pump prime

cards.q: A patient listed for valve surgery has a neutrophilia. What do you do?
cards.a: Cancel, and find and treat the source of infection.

importance.why: operating with active infection risks prosthetic valve endocarditis

cards.q: A CABG patient has a neutrophilia. When may surgery still go ahead?
cards.a: If WCC less than 12.0 and CRP normal, after discussion with the surgical team.

importance.why: threshold for proceeding with CABG

cards.q: How do you prepare a high-risk patient with respiratory impairment for cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Admit them for physiotherapy, nebulizers and education.

importance.why: optimisation reduces respiratory complications

cards.q: A patient's renal function deteriorates acutely before cardiac surgery. What do you do?
cards.a: Treat it before surgery: stop nephrotoxic drugs including ACE inhibitors; consider iv fluids.

importance.why: operating through acute kidney injury worsens renal outcome

cards.q: A patient on your list is MRSA positive. What do you do?
cards.a: Treat it preoperatively, consulting the infection control team for the appropriate treatment.

importance.why: MRSA wound and sternal infection are serious complications

cards.q: A lung lesion is found before CABG. How do you proceed?
cards.a: Investigate with a lateral film and CT; isolated non-infective lesions do not usually contraindicate coronary surgery.

importance.why: decides whether to proceed with CABG
